speechtext:

As the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has recently stated that if this country can overcome its annual trade deficit of more than S12 billion a year in fully manufactured products, we could make available an additional 800,000 new jobs for Canadians to work at, and as a vital aspect of increasing our exports of these very important products is to make Canadian producers more aware of the opportunities which exist for selling their products in the many export markets which are available to them, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis):

It has been announced that Statistics Canada, when providing its annual figures next month for changes in the consumer price index, intends to downplay the role of food prices as an element of that index by some 3.5 per cent.
Since the reason for making the change has to do with patterns of consumption which are now four years old-a smaller percentage of family income was spent upon food four years ago than is the case now-will the minister prevent this change which will have a profoundly misleading impact on the price index, given the fact that food prices have risen by almost 15 per cent so far this year?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Postmaster General, who should be aware of the situation in Orangeville, Ontario, where the local members of the Postal Workers Union wrote to a number of offices urging those workers to stay on the job in the national interest, and where the local workers in Orangeville reported for work on Monday and Tuesday and kept the office open, with the result that mail was delivered to some 12,000 homes in the area, only to find on Wednesday that on orders from Ottawa the postal management has decided to lock them out without pay.
I ask the Postmaster General how he can possibly justify this disgraceful betrayal of these dedicated and loyal employees.

Mr. Speaker, the incident at Orangeville was brought to my attention so that I could look into it. I feel the example of the employees there should have been followed by many other

postal workers throughout Canada. The only reason that decision was made was that, because of the strikes at other post offices, no mail was reaching Orangeville, and so they would have been given access to the building but without having any work to do. It was rather difficult for us to do so, under the circumstances; we therefore told them to go back home. It was not a matter of having what is known as a lock-out. We merely told them to return home and that we would call them back as soon as there was work to be done.
Shame!

Mr. Speaker, in six years I have never seen a more shameful performance by a minister. Does the minister deny it was the postal management at Ottawa with the advisory committee of the Post Office, of which the Postmaster General himself is a member, who decided upon the policy that these employees would be locked out, not only in Orangeville but in other areas where the postal workers had decided to go back to work and to keep the Post Office open, without pay?
Can the minister give an assurance to the House today that these dedicated and patriotic Canadians who work to serve the people in their communities will get full pay for the day they were locked out, and that this disgraceful circumstance will never be repeated in the future?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I can guarantee all those postal employees who want to work in our offices, where there is work to be done, that they will be welcome. We will give them work to do and they will be paid. I do not think a department or any responsible organization can be asked to pay employees when there is no work to do. Still, I feel that as time goes on, as more employees go back to work the more we shall be able to give them work to do.

Mr. Speaker, there was work for these employees to do and the Postmaster General should be aware of that. Never again can the government ask people to sacrifice in the national interest, by returning to work during a strike to provide an essential service, if they find they have been treated so shabbily.
Hear, hear!
Can the Postmaster General give the House firm assurance that the policy of lock-out has stopped as of today and that no postal employees in the country have been locked out by postal management?

Mr. Speaker, if the policy of lock-out has been existing, it will be stopped.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take the opportunity of this question to clarify a reply I gave a few moments ago? I asked the Deputy Postmaster General if there had been lock-outs anywhere in Canada. There have been no lock-outs up to now anywhere in the country, and therefore any employee who comes to work will be received and paid.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1978-79-80 MEASURE TO GRANT SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING POWER
speechtext:
that Bill C-7, to provide supplementary borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1978-79, to provide borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1979-80 and to amend the Financial Administration Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the borrowing authority bill now before the House seeks a supplementary borrowing authority
[Mr. Speaker.)
of $7 billion for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1979, and borrowing authority of $10 billion for fiscal 1979-80. This bill also seeks explicit authorization for the government to borrow in foreign currencies as well as Canadian dollars, and amends the Financial Administration Act so as to clarify that use of borrowing authority is calculated on a "net" basis.
As hon. members will recall, the government's cash requirements, exclusive of foreign exchange transactions, amounted to $8.3 billion in fiscal 1977-78, and the current fiscal year's cash requirements, exclusive of foreign exchange requirements, will be in the order of $11.8 billion, as I have said many times in the last few months.
In total, therefore, our domestic cash requirements for fiscal years 1977-78 and 1978-79 will be about $20.1 billion.
In addition to these cash requirements arising out of our domestic operations, the government has, during the last 12 months, arranged foreign borrowings of $750 million U.S. and $1.5 billion Deutschmarks, and has already arranged standby lines of credit of $5.5 billion U.S. These financial arrangements have been undertaken in order to add to Canada's international reserves and to provide assurance that the government is in a position to supplement the net inflow of capital into Canada.
As hon. members are aware, the government is now in the process of borrowing a further $750 million through the issuance of bonds on the U.S. market.
Let me now review the borrowing authorities that have been granted from March of 1977 to date, and against which borrowings in this period have been charged.
In March, 1977, borrowing authority of $7 billion was provided to meet anticipated cash requirements for fiscal year 1977-78. A further $9 billion borrowing authority was sought and provided as part of the income tax bill passed in December, 1977. Finally, on March 22, 1978, additional borrowing authority of $5 billion was granted.
This makes a two-year total borrowing authority of $21 billion which is not sufficient to meet the combination of domestic borrowings for the $20.1 billion in cash requirements for the two fiscal years ending next March 31, and our foreign borrowings to date of about $4.5 billion. Nor does it allow a margin to bring our borrowing authority in line with the amounts available under our already negotiated stand-by credit facilities.
As to our domestic debt program to date, during fiscal 1977-78 the Government of Canada raised in the Canadian markets about $3 billion net through the issue of Treasury Bills, about $3.4 billion net through the issue of marketable bonds, and about $1.7 billion net through the issuance of Canada Savings Bonds, for a total of about $8.1 billion.
During the current fiscal year to October 11, 1978, about $1.5 billion net has been raised domestically through the issue of Treasury Bills and $2.9 billion net through the issue of bonds in the Canadian markets.
October 19, 1978

The bill now before you requests supplementary borrowing authority of $7 billion to cover the balance of the domestic debt program for the current fiscal year, including a new series of Canada Savings Bonds, and as I have said, for the possibility to provide for further requirements in our foreign exchange transactions, including the use of our stand-by lines of credit.
The bill also provides borrowing authority of $10 billion for the new fiscal year beginning next April 1. We have previously indicated that cash requirements excluding foreign exchange transactions, are expected to be $9.7 billion for fiscal 1979-80. The government's cash balances at the beginning of the next fiscal year should be sufficient to allow part of the 1979-80 requirements to be met through a rundown in cash balances. The borrowing authority now being sought will thus provide a margin for contingencies.
Canadian dollars obtained by the government through the sale of foreign exchange reserves may eventually be needed in order to repurchase foreign exchange. For this reason the government intends to raise most of its domestic cash requirements in the Canadian capital markets rather than by running down its cash balances.
I would like now to turn to the section of the bill amending the Financial Administration Act. In the act as it now exists there is some uncertainty concerning the amount to be charged against the statutory borrowing authority in any period. This arises particularly in connection with short-term borrowings under the revolving stand-by lines of credit negotiated with Canadian chartered banks and international banks. When a borrowing is first made under a revolving stand-by credit pursuant to section 37 of the FAA, it is clearly a charge against the borrowing authority. At maturity date the borrower may wish to extend the borrowing for a further period immediately. Pursuant to section 38, this would not be a charge against the borrowing authority, because the borrowing is made to repay a maturing issue. Should the option be exercised after a delay, however, because of the manner in which section 38 is worded it may constitute a further charge against the borrowing authority.
This result would clearly restrict the full use and flexibility of the revolving stand-by lines of credit. The proposed amendment to the Financial Administration Act would clarify that it is only the net increase in outstanding debt from the date of the borrowing authority to the date of calculation of use of this authority that would be charged.

Mr. Speaker, the bill we are introducing in the House today aims at clarifying certain situations concerning financial administration and at increasing for the final months of fiscal year 1978-79 the borrowing authority of the government on financial markets, as well as at obtaining for fiscal year 1979-80, the authority to borrow up to $10 billion for government operations.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to move second reading of this bill. I want it to be referred as soon as possible to the
Borrowing Authority Act
committee, where myself and officials from my department will be able to provide hon. members with all the details they may require on this bill. During the past, such bills were generally introduced at the same time as the supplementary estimates. We are now introducing a bill directly in the House, which greatly simplifies the work of opposition members. Very often in the past, these authorizations were given on the same day as the supplementary estimates were passed, and very often-and rightly so in my opinion-hon. members complained that they did not have enough time to analyse these proposals. I therefore wanted to proceed immediately to the consideration of this important bill so as to obtain the required authority as soon as possible, and also to give hon. members the opportunity during consideration of this bill in committee to ask the questions which may concern them.

When the "emperor" first took power, this nation had less than $20 billion in total debt, which was costing us an average of 4.71 per cent interest. If this authority is now granted and if this government goes

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
ahead with the borrowings, which presumably it intends to go ahead with, we will find that the total debt in Canada will jump from the $20 billion to which I referred to $74 billion. Not only will that be the total debt, and the impact on future Canadians is obvious, but the interest rate will also rise from the 4.71 per cent to which I referred to an average of approximately 8 per cent.
What I am leading up to is that this House must come to grips with the economic blackhole which liberalism has sunk us into in the last 15 years. This government casually sought and obtained authority to borrow $7 billion in March of 1977. In December of 1977 this minister sought and obtained authority to borrow an additional $9 billion. In March of 1978 he sought and obtained authority to borrow another $5 billion. He added it up for us today. He said the total came to $21 billion. That is one figure he has right. Let us add the $17 billion he is requesting today, and we find that since March of 1977 this government has sought authority to borrow $38 billion. One thing which I think is perhaps often overlooked, or perhaps misunderstood, is that the authority which has been requested is additional authority. As the minister has made clear on previous occasions, any outstanding bonds can be re-financed, so what we are being asked to approve today is additional authority for $17 billion. On the minister's own admission, since March of 1977 the government has already received authority to borrow $21 billion.
Once again the minister has said that this bill should be expedited and passed quickly. This should arouse our interest. Why is it so important to interrupt the throne speech debate in order to put before this House a measure which is not an economic measure or a budgetary measure but which is a request that we quickly approve borrowing authority amounting to a further $17 billion? The reason I ask this is that I think this question of urgency shows the ad hoc nature of the dealings this government is engaged in, month in and month out.
I know that the minister is conveniently forgetful, but he did refer to authority which was obtained in 1977 and 1978, and it is interesting to go back through Hansard to see exactly what he said at that time as to what would be the effect of those borrowings and why they were needed.
The borrowing requested by the minister on November 7, 1977, is described by him at page 646 of Hansard for that date. The minister said that the government was rapidly running out of borrowing authority and that the government needed money for various reasons. He went on to say that it was vital to avoid any unnecessary delay in proceeding with the bill at that time. He said that, to a considerable extent, the economy depended on business confidence and that the measure then before us was extremely important in order to secure that confidence. At that time the government was seeking authority to borrow about $9 billion.
After describing that bill the minister went on to say that the increase in borrowing authority sought at that time was to

cover estimated financial requirements into the next fiscal year, and to provide a substantial margin for contingencies. We granted that authority on the understanding that it was not only enough to cover that fiscal year but that it would contribute a substantial amount for the next fiscal year.
That brings me to March 16, 1978. At page 3859 of Hansard for that date we find the debate on the new request for authority to borrow $5 billion. The minister had this to say:
The authority in this bill to borrow a further $5 billion, together with the unused portion of the $16 billion authority granted in March and December of 1977, should provide the government with sufficient borrowing powers to meet all cash requirements for the fiscal year 1978-79, and provide a margin as usual for contingencies.
Surely the House must ask this minister what went wrong? Why were we told in March that if we granted borrowing authority for $5 billion that that could be sufficient for the current fiscal year, when we now find that a further $7 billion is being requested? Think of the magnitude of what this minister has done. He told us in March that in the current year he needed a further $5 billion, and now we find that he needs an additional $7 billion. In view of what I have said, asking us to give speedy passage to this bill is absolutely irresponsible and an affront to this House.
Let me clarify one thing. Certainly most of us-I know I am one-cannot comprehend billions of dollars, but let us not allow that to distract us from the hard truth of what this government is doing.
This government has allowed its spending to get so out of control in relation to its revenue that we now have an ever-mounting deficit on the budgetary account which, in turn, has to be financed in one way or another. That is the simple truth. We are being asked to authorize borrowing of $7 billion for this current year and another $10 billion for the next one, and we are not being given the slightest indication as to what the picture will be in fiscal 1980. That is something we should not tolerate.
Where are the facts and figures? Why does the minister need this blanket borrowing authority of $10 billion for fiscal 1980, which is the period from April 1 of next year to March 31, 1980? The minister slipped into a press conference here in Ottawa, misled the press and tried to mislead the Canadian public by boldly saying that the government cut back its fiscal 1980 spending to $52.6 billion, that our cash needs are $9.7 billion and that "Isn't that great?" Hon. members will note that the minister did not reveal his revenue estimates for fiscal 1980. He did not make it clear to the press or to the Canadian public that, according to his own internal figures, revenue will be less than $40 billion, resulting in a shortfall, by the government's own figures, of $13.3 billion in fiscal 1980.

I do not want to draw any particular inference from this, but I find it very interesting that one advertising agency alone, on behalf of the Anti-Inflation Board, was paid $445,000 to tell us what inflation is all about. There is no mystery about where inflation comes from-we are dealing with it right here. It will come out of Bill C-7.
Inflation, basically, is the result of the government running too big a deficit, which in turn means it has to borrow funds, which in turn means the Bank of Canada has to borrow some of those funds, which increases the monetary system in the country and gives us the inflation. So how wonderfully odd it is that the government has spent $445,000 on McClaren Advertising which is telling us what causes inflation, without, presumably, realizing that that $445,000 will increase the government's deficit, which means it will have to borrow more money, which in turn creates more inflation in this country.

I wish Mr. Goldfarb had taken a trip to the far south or gone some place else, because the greatest thing that could have occurred, both economically and politically in this country, had Mr. Goldfarb not so instructed the Prime Minister, would have been for the Prime Minister to have tested the water some time this month or next month.

I think it is interesting to take a look at where the money we are now being asked to authorize was spent. Goldfarb picked up $100,000 of it-that was his fee for one assignment alone.
As I come to the Parliament Buildings every day, month in and month out, I watch the construction of the steps going down to the Bytown Museum. Even to my untrained eyes it looked like a pretty expensive job, but I must admit that when I asked what those steps cost-and there are about 40 of them-I was flabbergasted to find they cost $410,000-just steps to go down to the Bytown Museum a few months of every year.
There are various examples of what the government has been up to, Mr. Speaker. How many of us recall the $200,000 which was spent on a study to determine how long people spent in public washrooms? Let us not lose sight of that. Because the

government is now faced with a deficit, that $200,000 must be financed at 9 per cent, and every eight years that $200,000 doubles. The silly little study will cost the Canadian public $400,000 in eight years, and $800,000 in 16 years. As a result of that study, we have knowledge as to the amount of time used by males and females in public washrooms. As far as males are concerned, it was an average of 41 seconds, and as far as females are concerned, 75 seconds. This is the fiddling around that the government has been engaged in while the nation faces one of the most serious economic crises faced by any nation in the industrial world.
Not only must the minister explain more fully why this borrowing is needed, but he should deal with some other interesting questions. One such question relates to borrowing in foreign lands. There should be no doubt that clause 4 of the bill has a very good purpose. The money lords of Wall Street told this little minister that they wanted the authority of the Parliament of Canada behind the borrowing, that they do not trust him. They want parliament to confirm that the authorization to borrow $7 billion, and eventually $10 billion, is in fact backed by the Parliament of Canada, not just by a government which will hold office for a few further months.
The minister chose not to explain why the bill included an authority to borrow $10 billion in fiscal 1980. We know nothing about fiscal 1980. The House has been furnished with no figures. We do not know what the expenditure and revenue forecasts are, or what the budgetary deficit will be for that year. Why should we be asked to hand him blindly an authority to borrow $10 billion during that year? What is the rush? We know the government is planning an election. Perhaps it would be embarrassing in April or May of next year to request that $10 billion authority. If that is the only reason, I wish the government would admit it. It is not good enough simply to ask us to okay blindly a $10 billion authority without giving the usual, expected budgetary figures before any fiscal moves are made by parliament.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1978-79-80 MEASURE TO GRANT SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING POWER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1978-79-80 MEASURE TO GRANT SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING POWER
speechtext:
We must put into perspective how well or how poorly the country is doing. I could quote from many economists and analysts, but I should like to refer to the relevant quarterly report by Wood Gundy, the largest investment dealers in Canada. In September, 1978, that firm had the following to say about our economy:
Despite an official commitment by Prime Minister Trudeau to a 5 per cent real growth rate, our August Forecast looks to no more than a 3.3 per cent increase in real GNP this year, with the rate falling further to only 2.2 per cent in 1979. Some improvement is likely in 1980, largely as a result of a pickup in capital spending,... We therefore expect unemployment to worsen over the next two years, averaging 8.7 per cent in 1978 and 9.1 per cent in 1979 before moderating to 8.9 per cent in 1980.
We are being asked to give a borrowing authority for 1980, yet a reputable investment house told us that our economy will be so sluggish that there will be 9 per cent unemployment for the entire three years-1978, 1979 and 1980. We have ended up with huge deficits, huge debts and the highest unemployment since depression years. That is the culmination of this



October 19, 1978

black hole of Liberalism. That is how far the government has pulled the nation down in the 15 years of its rule.
It is important to analyse what this vicious inflationary spiral looks like. We find that the federal government incurs deficits which must be financed by selling securities. The government has found that it can no longer sell sufficient securities in the Canadian domestic market, because obviously interest rates are driven up the more that is done. Thus the government resorts to selling securities to foreigners in foreign currencies. There are only three other countries in the world which resort to such financing to cover consumption deficits in their home economies. Those three countries are Zaire, Panama and Spain. That is the level to which our economy has been dragged by the government extending our borrowing into foreign jurisdictions.
This is a serious matter, because when a debt in foreign currency is incurred, one must speculate as to how much that debt will be currencywise when it is time for repayment. For example, the German loan which was incurred in May of this year provided a little less than $800 billion Canadian. It would cost an additional $130 million Canadian to repay that loan today. The government undertook to repay that amount of interest when it borrowed the $800 million Canadian. The more we borrow in foreign currency, the more the risk will be extended.
The minister should have come into the House requesting a $17 billion borrowing authority to put capital investments into place. What would $17 billion do? I understand that it would build 150,000 homes in Canada. Perhaps it would build two Alaska pipelines.
Now that the government basically has drained the domestic market, it is resorting to borrowing foreign funds to cover consumption deficits in the country. Deficits are being incurred which result in financing by selling securities. Then the Bank of Canada is forced to buy many of the securities to stabilize the market and to ensure a success as far as government issues are concerned. In so doing, the Bank of Canada pumps reserves into the banking system, which leads to a multiplied level of money and credit in the system. Excessive credit expansion then leads to a long trend in declining liquidity among our banks and corporations, which raises the level of risk which, together with the continuing rise in loan demand, raises the level of interest rates through the economy.
That is the cycle they are putting us through, Mr. Speaker. In our late stage of liquidity deterioration, companies have become less able to withstand business downturns; they are less resilient on the recovery. This is demonstrated by our increasing level of bankruptcies, especially among small businesses. According to Dun and Bradstreet, in the first six months of this year bankruptcies were up 40 per cent over last year. Bankruptcies in Canada have jumped to the point that today, rather than having one bankruptcy in Canada for every ten in the United States, the ratio one would normally expect, we
Borrowing Authority Act
have seven bankruptcies in Canada for every ten in the United States.
The problem caused by the federal government's massive federal funding is also reflected in our mortgage field. This week we have seen interest rates on mortgages go still higher. We are also faced with a rising foreclosure rate in home mortgages. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, for example, paid out insurance claims on 1,051 residential units to the end of August this year, against 405 for the whole of last year.
I would suggest that fiscal discipline has clearly broken down at both the cabinet and administrative levels of government. This is partly a problem of philosophies that must be changed, and it is partly a problem of structure which must also be altered. A general election will presumably rectify the problem of philosophy, but even here one important barrier to any solution is the lack of understanding by many voters of the true origins of inflation to Canada. And not only inflation, but all the other problems associated with that phenomenon.
Not only has the government misled the Canadian public concerning the causes of our inflation-high unemployment, lack of real growth, and current account deficits-but this misrepresentation has been pounded home by the New Democratic Party who have deliberately told the Canadian public that we need more of what has already made the nation so sick.
If there were a better public understanding that it is the national cumulative deficit, the public debt, which becomes our public debt, that has caused inflation, people would not be picketing supermarkets, but would be picketing the Parliament Buildings. They would not complain to their members of parliament about taxes, they would complain about the Bank of Canada building that has been a-building for five years at a cost of $53 million. They would be complaining about the mammoth spending programs launched by this government.
There is something we must not lose sight of, Mr. Speaker. Year after year we subsidize the CBC. It has cost the nation over $3 billion in total. To the degree that the government has to finance those subsidies, it is now putting us on the treadmill of not only having to pay for the initial subsidy but to pay 9 per cent interest per year. That is what it has led us into, Mr. Speaker.
We must bear in mind that higher taxes and inflation are only the symptoms; spending is the problem with this government. In the short term the government must go on a diet to avoid a severe coronary later on. In the long term, structural and philosophical changes are required.
In the United States the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1970 makes it necessary for the administrative branch in that government to price out the cost for new legislation for five years into the future. We need that approach here, not only for new legislation but for old.
In the past 15 years all governments in Canada have increased their share of the GNP by over one-third. Let me repeat that, Mr. Speaker. In the past 15 years all governments

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
in Canada have increased their share of the GNP by over one third. No other industrialized nation has had that type of escalation in governments' take. One half of this spending is at the federal level. In terms of actual levels of spending, the federal government's expenditures will amount to $52.6 billion in 1980, compared to $6.4 billion in 1960, an eightfold increase in 20 years.
In a recent special study by the C. D. Howe Institute, H. V. Kroeker summarizes his suggested improvements which I think we should consider. He said:
Ultimate control of, and accountability for, the expenditures of government must be exercised by the legislature. The Canadian House of Commons is hampered, however, in effectively carrying out this role because it has not adapted quickly enough to the demands placed on modern government. To enhance and reinforce parliament's role requires a number of improvements which parallel those proposed for the internal expenditure process of the federal government. These improvements include-
He then itemizes a list of things he would like to see improved. One is a general assessment of past and future trends of government expenditures covering a span of ten years, five years into the past and five years into the future. He would also like to see the preparation of the economic basis on which future projections have been made, such as the expected rates of growth in the gross national product, rates of unemployment, inflation, wage increases and so on. He would like to see the preparation of comprehensive government overviews of programs, along with an indication of how these relate to government policy and other programs. He would like to see the introduction of the right of parliamentary committees to investigate, at their initiative, matters that fall under their mandate, and to call public servants as witnesses on technical matters or in relation to the implementation and funding of programs. He would like to see the creation of a parliamentary committee on economic and expenditure policy to review longer term projections and trends, and finally, he would like to see the introduction of the accounting-officer concept as part of the mandate of the public accounts committee. I think these things, or perhaps modifications of them, are badly needed.
This is getting out of hand. It is not a matter of trivial deficits any longer; it is a matter of the government literally being able to finance out of current revenue only 75 cents of every dollar it is spending. Yet I do not see the slightest indication by this government, and certainly not by the minister, of an attempt to facilitate the types of review I have summarized and which, presumably, have been endorsed by the C. D. Howe Institute.
In his contribution to the throne speech debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that we ranked sixth or seventh behind various other countries. Presumably that was an attempt to contradict what we in this party have often said, that we have dropped from second to seventh in the world, but I think he had in mind that first, second and third were Kuwait and countries like that. Just the odd time the Prime Minister is of help. In his speech he listed the six countries that are actually ahead of us. If we take the Prime Minister's six, plus the six we were referring to-West Germany, Belgium,

the United States, Norway-we would find that we are thirteenth. Something must have got through to the Prime Minister. In fact Canada has dropped to thirteenth, if you include the countries he named, compared to second-

I wish him well in it, but I suggest that if he needs any more information he should go to the Prime Minister for it. He knows the names of the other six countries which are also ahead of us.
This is what we are faced with in this bill, Mr. Speaker. We are faced with the fact that the government only last spring told us they needed $5 billion more borrowing authority to get them out of this year. Now in October they find they need another $7 billion, and they want specific authority to borrow part of that $7 billion in a foreign currency. They have even gone further and said, "For good measure, throw in another $10 billion for fiscal 1980; we will probably need that too."
Obviously, the situation is out of control. I believe that we must, in order to put it into perspective, vote against what the government is asking us to approve. Before I sit down I intend to move a motion. My motion will be that we not now read this bill but that it be considered objectionable in principle for the mere fact that the government is requesting us to grant an authority for massive borrowing in a future fiscal year and yet we have no proper budgetary presentation to allow us to judge whether that authority should be granted or not. But, Mr. Speaker, in truth we need some figures. We need information. Why did this borrowing authority request come before the budget? Surely the proper sequence would have been to bring in the budget, let us see whatever figures the minister is willing to put before us, and let us then come to our own conclusion whether a borrowing authority of $17 billion is warranted.
We know the reason for the urgency. They are in trouble. They are in trouble in New York because they have to satisfy some legal firms in New York that they have the authority to borrow the money they would like to borrow now. That is why they want to put this bill through. Surely they owe it to us to give us a lot more detail. They owe it to us to show us, for example, what the future trends are in Canada, assuming that they allow this 9 per cent increase per year to follow up to, say, 1984, and revenues to continue to grow. If those figures are projected, it will be found they are very startling. One will find that the budgetary deficit, rather than contracting, is going to get bigger year by year. In short, if the government can only be as restrained as they indicated in their press conference, and if revenues are maintained at the level that they have been in recent years, the deficit in 1984 will be considerably bigger than it is today, and today it is totally unacceptable.
Put it again into perspective. This government have the audacity to hint or to say that they are being restrained, and
October 19, 1978

yet they admit that the deficit is somewhere around the $10 billion level. That deficit in relation to our federal government spending is triple the deficit that the United States government is living with now. It is triple in relation to our spending compared to the American deficit in relation to their spending. The Americans are worried. But I do not sense that this government are worried about anything other than getting re-elected. That is all they are concerned about. Whether the country is economically in good shape or bad shape becomes secondary to them in their anxiety to try to win favour once again with the Canadian electorate.
In closing, perhaps Thomas Jefferson, many years ago, put this type of situation squarely. He said:
I place economy among the first and most important virtues, and public debt as the greatest of dangers ... we must make our choice between economy and liberty, or profusion and servitude. If we can prevent the government from wasting the labors of the people under the pretense of caring for them, they will be happy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the idea of borrowing $17 billion must really do something to the imagination of the people who contemplate it. If we have to borrow that kind of money, something is seriously wrong in this society.
One has to look at the need to borrow the money. There is no question that, faced with the kind of slackness in the economy that we have, a deficit under the present circumstances is probably unavoidable, and that the alternative to not having a deficit and having a balanced budget-and I am not sure that my friends to the right are suggesting that we have a balanced budget-would be to make the unemployment rate of the thirties look like a picnic.
As a matter of public policy the borrowing has to be carried out. But it is sad to think that this is the only way it can be done.
While I was listening to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) use the figures from Woods, Gordon, an interesting thought occurred to me. The thought did not occur to me when my own leader was using those figures the other day.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1978-79-80 MEASURE TO GRANT SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING POWER
speechtext:
Thank you. It is the same thing for Wood Gundy because Woods, Gordon is somewhat tainted with Liberal tendencies; Wood Gundy is not. Therefore, it makes it more useful to talk about Wood Gundy.
I presume Wood Gundy have been reading the polls, like everyone else, and I presume that they are making the assumption that perhaps the Liberals will not be in office in 1980 and that the Conservatives will be in office then. Yet despite that kind of possibility, Wood Gundy is saying that "we are still following the same disastrous course that we are on at present." With that in mind, I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe has one or two conclusions to reach. First, his party is not going to form the government in 1980, and Wood Gundy is making these predictions based on the Liberals remaining there and continuing their policies. Second, they are going to form the government, and it isn't going to make a damn bit of difference if they do or not, because the predictions are not going to be changed. That is really the point I want to make.
When one looks at $17 billion one has to ask and tell oneself that this is a serious problem. When you deal with the magnitude of that problem, what sort of suggestions are made as to the cause of it? We hear about a misspending of $5 million on telegrams, $17 million on courier services, and $400,000 to an advertising agency. Even when you add up all these little figures, you do not come anywhere close to $17 billion.
Even assuming there is some waste and mismanagement, as there tends to be in all large organizations, the way to correct it is not simply by being more efficient in government. As desirable as that may be, it is not going to knock out the $17 billion loan requirement.
When we talk about the economy it reminds me of a skit that sometimes appears over television. I think "The Honey-mooners" used to use it. Someone walks in and goes over to the stove. When he turns it on, instead of getting a flame, he gets a shot of water in the face. When he rushes into the bathroom and flushes the toilet he gets the triumphant march from "Aida" bursting forth in the living room. Something is not working. The whole economy is mixed up. The blue plumbers are sent for. They come with their wrenches and tinker with it. The whole system breaks down, and there is water all over the place. That is like the shape of our economy. It just is not working. Something is dramatically wrong with our economy and it will not be corrected by looking at an advertising or telegraph expenditure, or something similar.
The importance for parliament in trying to deal with this subject is to look at some of the underlying causes and some of the choices that face us with regard to what we can do with the economy. We have the blue choice, the one put forward by my

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
friends on my right, that the only thing wrong is with the present government and the fact that government expenditures are out of control.
We also have a pink choice, the choice of the New Democratic Party, as to what can be done. We feel that the problem is not in government expenditures. The problem is essentially that the market system in this society has broken down. It will not be corrected by the government getting out of and not managing the economy. That would only make it worse.
We have reached the point in the development of our society where we need more government management, rather than less. To the extent that the private sector has failed, and it has failed, the public sector has to take up the slack.
In that regard I must ask my friend from York-Simcoe if he really meant what he said when he stated that if the government were borrowing $17 billion for housing, it would be a different matter. I presume he is saying he would support a $17 billion public expenditure on the part of the government. If it is for current needs, he will not support it; but if it is for investment, he will. I am not sure he meant that and, therefore, I do not know why he introduced it.
Let us look at some of the problems and how this government and, to a very large extent, my friends on the right would handle it. At the moment we have a need to bolster the Canadian dollar. There are a number of ways in which that can be done. The government has chosen to increase rates for the fifth time.
What is the consequence of increasing interest rates in order to keep money in Canada? They have come to the conclusion that much of the devaluation of the Canadian dollar is because of the outflow of capital and the importance of inflowing capital. Raising interest rates has not worked in the past and it will not work now. However, the government is going to do that in order to stop some of the outflow. The consequence will be to slow down the whole economy. Raising interest rates will slow down the housing industry, investment, and all those other things about which they are concerned. The justification will probably be they had no choice, there was nothing else for them to do.
But there is a choice in these matters. It is not an easy choice or a perfect choice. However, it is preferable to raising interest rates. 1 refer to imposing exchange controls. I think the problem is that there is too much money in this country for gainful investment. The government have been too generous to people with high incomes, to people in businesses, particularly in the large business sector, and they have more money than they know what to do with. It is leaving the country for that reason. It must be stopped. There is a responsibility on those who make their money in this country to have some response to national needs.
The figures that we have bear out where the problem is. I agree the trade deficit is important and that it has something to do with it. However, what is more important is the fact that so much money is leaving the country in large amounts. Small amounts, such as those for people going on holidays or buying

a home in Florida, are not the real cause of the problem. Rather, it is that there are large sums of money leaving the country in an attempt to find more gainful interest rates somewhere else.
If we look at the section of the quarterly estimates, the Canadian balance of equal payments, page 56, under the heading of "Interest and Dividends", we can make a comparison. In 1969 we had a deficit on that account of $915 million. In 1977 the deficit was $3,480 million, almost four times as much in eight years, leaving this country.
When I discussed this matter with the people at Statistics Canada in order to try to get an accurate picture they said they could not give an accurate picture because the statistics were not good enough. They had to lump it under various headings, and they were not sure how much was private money and how much was business money.
They have an item called "Net Errors and Omissions", a very exact thing. Under that heading is shown a deficit of $219 million in 1969, whereas, in 1977 the outflow was $2,746 million, an incredible increase.
If you look at the offsetting amount of capital coming into Canada you find that, while it has increased, and I do not want to put the figures now, it has not increased at nearly the same rate as the outflow of money from this country.
Money does not flow out of the country just because there is no confidence. Anyone who does not have confidence in this country has to be out of his mind! I cannot think of any country in the world that has a more brilliant future than Canada. Any investor who does not see that does not deserve to be called an investor.
You cannot say this money is leaving Canada because there is no confidence in this country. It is leaving for other reasons. I suggest it is leaving because of public mismanagement. There is so much money around that it is just trying to find a place to light down. It moves back and forth on a quarter per cent rise in the interest rate.
The liquidity in large corporations is so great that some of these corporations make more money by placing their money for interest than they do on their own operations. A lot of this has arisen because of the very generous capital allowances we have allowed to large corporations. It has increased the liquidity and enabled them to do this kind of thing.
This is the kind of thing we have to examine. Therefore, you impose exchange controls. The minute you say that, however, someone says, "That means that if I want to go on a holiday I cannot do it without going to a bank or agency." But you do not have to do it that way and in most countries where there are exchange controls it is not done that way.
You can impose these controls on any sum of money over $50,000 in order to ensure the large sums of money-those that are affecting these figures-are taken into account. It will be much more desirable to try to deal with the dollar problem in this way than to keep raising interest rates in a losing battle of one-upmanship with the United States. This is a battle we
October 19, 1978

cannot win. Why is it not done? It is not done because the government does not want to manage the economy.
It is not easy to impose exchange controls. It means a government has to accept responsibility, and the present administration does not want to accept that kind of responsibility and it is this reluctance to do so that is at the heart of our economic problems.
The government has been cutting taxes over the years. One of the reasons we have borrowed to this extent is because the government has cut taxes, but they have cut them for the wrong people! The cuts have stimulated saving by those at the higher income levels. Taxes were cut for the more fortunate to such an extent that the people concerned could not spend all their money. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) himself said we were saving ourselves into a depression.
The New Democratic Party has said that cutting taxes might be necessary in the short term but, if taxes were to be cut, they should be cut for those at the lowest income levels so as to help those with consumption needs. In that way we derive a double benefit. Surplus funds are not created and the extra purchasing power stimulates the economy, putting people back to work. Revenue from taxes is greater, and the deficit is reduced at the same time. This is not only a more decent way to do things, it is a more efficient way. Why is it not being done? Because it means you have to make a decision in favour of the poor rather than the rich and at the moment there seems to be a blue tide running-the people who "have it made" are insisting on retaining their position, a position endorsed by the government.
It is not only tax benefits that are greater at higher income levels. The trend to more favoured treatment extends to such things as registered retirement savings plans and various other premiums. The Minister of Finance has, on occasion, pointed out that it is not just the rich who benefit from these programs. He tells us that some people from the middle income levels also benefit. But the benefits to the rich are disproportionate to the small amounts received by those at the lower end of the scale as a result of which the system works to increase savings at a time when we really need an increase in consumption.
The only solution proposed by hon. members to my right is that we should cut the public sector. Mr. Speaker, cutting the public sector simply exacerbates the problem. We are all familiar with examples of too much fat in the public sector, and to the extent that this is identifiable it should be cut out. But that is not the mood of those who sit on the government benches. Their idea of cutting the public sector is not to trim the fat but to make cuts across the board on principle, and this principle might be described, more or less in these words: we are going to get out of the economy, we are going to show the people we do not want to be in the economy, we are going to leave room for the private sector.
The other day my leader asked the Minister of Finance whether it was true that a recent study showed that the cuts made by the government would result in close to 100,000 being
Borrowing Authority Act
unemployed. The minister had to do some mental gyrations before answering that question. He attempted to demonstrate that by making 100,000 people unemployed in the public sector he would create jobs in the private sector. Yet the hon. gentleman has himself expressed disappointment with the performance of the private sector in this regard. Every time cuts were made on the assumption that the private sector would take up the slack, it did not happen. Unfortunately, the private sector increases the problem instead of diminishing it.
How could anyone in his right mind conclude that just because the government stops employing people the private sector would suddenly develop confidence and hire them? Business does not expand its operations in proportion to the number of employees the government has dismissed. The only reason business expands is because there is a market for what it is trying to sell, or the services it is providing. The actions of the government in this area are of no consequence to a businessman beyond becoming the subject, possibly, of conversation at the golf club.
We have much more compelling difficulties to face. It seems to me we are living in one kind of society, a society we think we understand, while moving rapidly into another kind of society, one we do not understand and one for which the government is not prepared. The government is attempting to manage by crisis, by election dates, and the official opposition is not being of much help in that regard though one would not expect them to be. The reason we find ourselves in this great economic difficulty is our reluctance to face the fact that the world is changing before our eyes and that the solutions we were once able to apply are no longer as useful as they were.
It seems to me that when we debate as parliamentarians we should try to understand the changes which are taking place and to listen to arguments in favour of one course of action as against other courses of action, arguments, if you like, of a philosophic nature; I recognize that philosophy is regarded as somehow unparliamentary, but I feel, nevertheless, that parliament should be a forum for philosophy. A great many things are changed in our society.
My hon. friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), reviewed what has happened in our society, when he spoke last week. He spoke of the changes that have taken place, many of them because of the presence of a social democratic party in Canada. There can be no comparison between the society into which he was born-and into which I was born for that matter- and the society we see today. For want of a better term, we call it the "welfare state". Nobody is going to dismantle the welfare state because, whatever faults it may possess, we are not willing to go back to the kind of jungle which existed before, in all its insensitivity. In our desire to be a more humane civilization we have removed many of the pressures which pushed civilization in a certain direction. We have removed combative presssures; pressures of poverty and pressures of illness and desperation.

This is not a desperate society. It is not the world of Adam Smith, if there ever was such a world. It is not a world of small shopkeepers competing against each other. We have a different society. Because it has been gradual and because we have fought every step of the way in order to attain this society, we have not stopped to analyse and ask what the implications are for the future, now that we have this kind of society. Ours is not the only welfare state. I do not think there is a country in the western world, including the United States, which does not devote much of its resources to the field of medicine, education or pensions, all of which are associated with welfare states.
Another thing that is happening is that growth in the western world is slowing down. That is not so just in Canada, but in the whole western world. Those of us who have been travelling to Japan, Germany, France, Britain, or even Sweden, will note that the preoccupation of those countries is the same as the preoccupation here: what happened to growth? What we tend to forget is that we have come through a period of the most rapid growth in human history. The last 30 or 40 years have been a period of incredible growth. This is not usual for the world. The world did not grow at that rate before, but because we have been living in this period we think it is going to go on forever. But suppose it is not going to go on forever, and suppose we simply have to adjust to making a decent society which is not constantly being prodded and pushed into consumption? I think that is in fact what is happening.
If we look around at people today, we find that they have changed a great deal. Their attitudes toward clothing, cars, and security have changed. Out of the old society a new one is emerging. The great difficulty is that, whatever we say about the old society, it is both true and false. Whatever we say about the new society is both true and false. But a government which continues to ignore the fact that it has a double problem, how to manage the existing society, and how to make the transition to the other one, is doomed to failure.
I will give some examples of failure. The government cuts taxes. I say the cuts are being made in the wrong places. Perhaps that is part of the failure, but it is a general failure in a relatively affluent society and in a welfare state. The Keynesian idea is that if we cut taxes we stimulate demand enormously, but instead, when we turn on the stove, we get a shot of water in the face, and the government stands there wondering what happened. Governments think they are doing the right thing but then wonder what happened.

speechtext:
The government still has not shown that it understands the problems sufficiently to forget about tax cuts and to initiate other things such as grants, payments, increased

old age pensions, increased family allowances, or earlier retirements, as ways to stimulate the economy.
Increases in public expenditures are positive and direct, and the outcome can be predicted. We are now entering a slow growth period. I do not want to go into all the reasons we are in a slow growth period, but I think we will have to face the fact that we will not continue to grow at the same pace as we have. To some extent we should not deplore that. We grew too fast for too long, and very often we grew at the expense of humanity and the environment, and people no longer want to do that. We are becoming a more stable society, and we have to make the necessary adjustments.
There is far less demand today for traditional goods and far more demand for services. This is becoming quite obvious, and it has an effect. Much of the inflation we experience in our society is a direct consequence of the switch from the production of goods. Productivity figures are totally misleading because they do not take this factor into account. When we switch from the production of goods to the consumption of services, we have what amounts to a productivity drop, because in providing services we cannot use labour-saving devices and inventions to the same extent as we can in the production of goods. Therefore we have what looks like a productivity drop.
As people in the goods sector increase their incomes, usually in line with productivity increases, which cannot be matched by the service sector, and the service sector wants to catch up-it is about 60 per cent of our economy now-that catchup is inflationary. That may be fair and just, but it is inflationary. A permanent inflation is built into a society which is in the process of this kind of transition. We hear very little about the consequences of that and of what needs to be done.
I am proud that my colleagues have had an important role to play in the redistribution policies of the last 30 years. Looking back now, redistribution in those years was relatively painless because people's incomes were growing very rapidly, and the gross national product was increasing enormously. This enabled our society to improve the situation of virtually everyone, not on a relative basis, but on an absolute basis. In addition, those who had some of their money taken away did not find it too painful because they were still improving their situations, and therefore we were able to effect redistribution domestically as well as internationally. But, what happens when the gross national product does not rise at the same rate? We get a right-wing conservative reaction because, in order to redistribute, something must be taken away from somebody, and people do not like that.
The money cannot come out of the surplus any more. There really must be a redistribution of existing resources. Some people must be told that they cannot become as rich as they did before, because some of the wealth has to be set aside for those who are not as well off. Then we go through this painful experience of moving to the right because people start to feel the effects of redistribution.

I think that there are now two moves taking place. We all know that there is a move to the right. Those of us who are in politics experience that, but I think the results in Saskatchewan, and the election of an NDP federal member of parliament in Newfoundland, indicate that there is also a willingness on the part of the public to look at more progressive ideas, if they are articulated. We are hoping to have the kind of debate in which there is no room in the middle, where the Liberals find themselves. They are right in the middle, trying to be all things to all people, and I do not think that is possible any more. We must take a stance on these changes which are taking place in our society, and decide which way we want to go. Should we stand in the way of these changes, or move with them and make the transition to a different kind of society?
We can call this society anything we want. We can call it the conserver society, as some people have, the post-industrial society or, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did, the new society. One of the few times the Prime Minister has been right in the last four years was in a speech he made a couple of years ago when he said that our society is changing. The idea of a Liberal Prime Minister finding that he is on the right side of history is enough to shock him back to reality and to go back to where he was before. The Prime Minister could not take it for very long, but our world is in fact changing. A new world is coming, and it will be a reasonably good world, as long as we adjust to it.
The reason the government seems so helpless in the face of what is happening is that it is not taking the dramatic changes into account as we become a new society. The government is still trying to deal entirely with the society which is dying away.
What is clear when we talk about this new society-it is easy to talk about a new society-is that more and more people who are looking at it are saying that the market system is breaking down. It should be obvious that we are not talking, as I said earlier, about Adam Smith's small shopkeepers; we are talking about large scale multinational corporations that can set their own prices and that, in fact, are sometimes bigger than governments and act as if they were governments. We are talking about large combinations of workers, not workers acting in isolation, workers protected by trade unions whose decisions affect hundreds of thousands of people, not just one man, two men or half a dozen men and women. This is a different kind of world.
We are talking about the welfare state where people no longer want to live by the law of an economic jungle. It operates at both levels; domestically and internationally. To some extent the only market that is left is the international market, and again some interesting things are happening there. What is happening is that, as the result of the spread of technology around the world, we are competing with everyone and nobody has a comparative advantage any more except in a very few things. We are competing internationally.

What is happening when we compete internationally? The very people who talk about competition in the domestic society are saying, "Protect us internationally. We do not want to compete with Taiwan, with Korea or with Singapore. We do not want to be thrown to the winds of international competition." The fact is that most of us are not and will not be.
A new kind of co-operative arrangement has to develop. In some ways a reverse colonialism is taking place. For centuries the west derived a net benefit from trade with the third world, with underdeveloped countries. We grew richer at the expense of the underdeveloped countries. Now the shoe is on the other foot. There is a real transfer of income from the western world to the third world. This is very obvious when you come to the oil producing countries; it is less obvious when you look at other countries. While this transfer of income does not show up as a per capita increase in wealth among the populations of those countries because their birth rate is so phenomenal, there is a real transfer of wealth from the west, and it is no longer in jute bags. Because of the multinationals and because of the foreign aid we have provided, we have given technology to many countries in the world.
We do not have much in the way of comparative advantage any more, nor does any other country have it. The Swedes and the Americans complain about it. It has to be faced that not only must we reorganize our internal economies to take into account the changes that are taking place, but we also have to do it internationally, otherwise there will be serious conflicts in that area as well.
What is the answer? No one is certain what the answer is beyond knowing that what they are doing now is not worth a darn, and what is being proposed by my friends on the right is no help either. For all practical purposes it does not represent any real kind of change. It seems to me that the problem is the same as it has always been, except that it is more acute, more urgent, more compelling, and we have to seek redistribution at two levels. Not just redistribution at the level of income. Certainly that will help, it is necessary, and it should be done. Now we are faced with the problem of redistribution of jobs as well. In his book entitled "Social Limits to Growth", Fred Hirsh talks about positional goods.
There are hundreds of thousands of bright young people coming out of university for whom there are no jobs. You can tell them to go pick apples or go pick tobacco-maybe there are jobs in those areas. But is this why we sent them to school? Is this why we told them to get an education? How can we ask people to do that? We can ask them to do it for a short period of time-and certainly it does not do anyone harm to do any kind of work because all work is worth-while-but the frustration of that kind of situation is becoming very obvious.
I think that much of the problem we have in the Post Office today arises from the fact that many of the people who work in the Post Office came out of school with a good education. They are not people who came out with just grade two or

I think it is that level of personal frustration, that struggle for an assertion of the dignity to which they think they are entitled, that is creating problems in the Post Office and, I think, in many other occupations as well. There will have to be a sharing of power. A rise in the number of neighbourhood groups, of citizens' participation, is an indication of the fact that people want to share. They feel they need to have more than just goods alone. They need to have access to good positions, to stature, to where the power is. For instance, look at an MP's job. It is not a bad job in many ways, but it is not the greatest job in terms of how hard we have to work for the money we make in comparison with other jobs. Presumably if we did as my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, would have us do, that is, reduce our salaries below what they are now-

They do it because there is something more in life than just money. They do it because they feel that they are useful to society, that they make a contribution, and that they are where some of the power is, though again we might not have as much power as we think.
What this leads to is not that the government should get out of the economy, and not that they should say, "We will turn it back to the private sector", because this cannot be done. I saw my friend, Lubor Zink, earlier today in the corridor. He would say, "I told you so; you cannot have a little bit of socialism. There is no such thing as a little bit of socialism". I think he is right; we cannot go on the way we have. We need a managed economy, and we need the government in the economy rather than out.
