The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-7, to provide supplementary borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1978-79, to provide borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1979-80 and to amend the Financial Administration Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take a few minutes of this House to give my opinion on Bill C-7 introduced this morning, which did not give us much time to consider it in detail. We did not take much time to consider it because it is not long. When the news was announced yesterday I thought that it was a borrowing of $7 billion. But I realize from reading the bill that borrowing authority is requested for $17 billion and when 1979 will be over the government will have borrowed a total of $28 billion, and that will increase greatly the debt of the country. Mr. Speaker, we have already made several borrowings to bolster the dollar, that famous floating dollar which has been diving like a submarine. The latest borrowings are for $750 million.
I am talking about the bond issue worth $750 million to bolster the dollar, and more recently, about another loan of $1.14 billion for the same purpose, which means that if we add up all the loans issued to prop up the dollar, we reach a total of $4.5 billion. Mr. Speaker, I find these loans enormous. Even then, our dollar has not been saved. If only the dollar had been bolstered and had regained its normal value, but this is not happening.
Mr. Speaker, this is another proof of the falseness of our debt system. For 15 years, we have been coming to this House and telling the government that it is time to get out of this system of running up debts continuously. After all, what are we now doing? We have to borrow to pay off old debts. We simply put the account in another name. The only difference will be that the interest charges will increase. Instead of paying 7 per cent or 7.5 per cent as before, we will pay 10 per cent, 10.5 per cent or 15 per cent and even more. This little game has been going on since the beginnings of Canada, to such a point that we are now saying that a debt is an asset. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I have never believed that getting into debt was becoming the owner of anything. I consider that I own something when I no longer owe anything on it and when it is no longer mortgaged.
Canada is now mortgaged for over $67 billion, and if we add the $28 billion to that, we will have reached $95 billion at the end of 1979. That is a mortgage. No one should say that we
Borrowing Authority Act
own Canada. We do not. We are living with a great many debts which we cannot repay because we will have to borrow each year if not each month to pay the interests one the old debts. We no longer have enough even to pay off the interests. We must borrow to do so. Where will all this lead us, Mr. Speaker? I suggest that it will simply lead to a crash such as occurred in the thirties, which was caused by the fact that the government had completely lost control over the Canadian money supply. I say that is what we are heading for today. The Bank of Canada controls absolutely nothing. It seems to control the amount of debts, but with all the changes made in the Bank of Canada, even though it has raised the bank rate to 1014 per cent on the reserves, that does not bother the chartered banks one bit because when they run out of money, they could not care less; they do not need the Bank of Canada: they go to the client, because today the client who borrows can create the bank reserves.
That is what is happening today. Let no one say that the Bank of Canada is going to control the chartered banks by imposing 1014 per cent on illegal reserves, when they fall below the allowed amount. In any event, the 10'A per cent applies only for three days because we know full well that after three days, the chartered banks go to their clients to borrow the $500 the latter will deposit in their savings account and on which the banks will pay 9 per cent interest.
It does not take long to build up reserves. That is how it works, Mr. Speaker, and today we try to cope with our debt. The issue should be studied in depth because there is an inconsistency in Canada. Our country is the largest borrower in the world and one of the most industrialized countries having the largest debt per capita. See if you can understand that! We have the largest debt per capita. To my mind it is because the government does not take its responsibility which is to control credit in Canada. This is the reason of the problem.
As I said earlier, we are on the path of another crisis like in the thirties. Let us remember what happened in the thirties. The government had lost all control over the issue of credit and money and at that time every chartered bank was allowed to print its own money, provided it kept gold in its vaults. Eager to make profits like others, they did not care whether or not they had gold in their vaults; even if they had no gold left they printed money, they issued credit and they granted loans. When they realized there was nothing left, they kept on lending anyway. Then, there was the crash of the thirties and who saved the situation?
Mackenzie King saved the situation by creating the Bank of Canada in 1935. In the Bank of Canada Act, it was prescribed that henceforth no chartered bank would be allowed to print money. That goes for legal currency, but our monetary system is divided into two parts: a legal currency which we call our

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
dollar and monetary credit. But the legal currency represents only 8 per cent and the monetary credit 92 per cent of the money supply.
Mackenzie King did the right thing when he put the issue of monetary credit and legal currency under the control of the Bank of Canada. Only the Bank of Canada-and it is still the same today and it has stabilized the monetary system at that time-issues the currency, the paper money and the coinage, and if the chartered banks need some, they must buy it from them. The Bank of Canada is the sole authority and has complete control over all this. So much for the 8 per cent of the paper currency. However, he had forgotten a small detail. It may have been intentional, but he had forgotten a detail.
If he had done the same thing in the same legislation for the monetary credit, if he had instructed the Bank of Canada to control monetary credit as closely, the new credit for the new production that has to be minted by the bank each year, if the same act had been applied to monetary credit, we would not be in trouble as we are today. Indeed not, and I think several members will agree with me. It is realized today that if we are in debt up to the eyes, it is because the Bank of Canada has never controlled monetary credit, has never minted the yearly production. Never! It has left it to the chartered banks. The chartered banks are the ones that mint the production.
Let us suppose that last year we had $75 billion in gross national product and $40 billion in national revenue. This amounts to $35 billion in new products which must be minted. This is what is called minting new credit. If the Bank of Canada had any authority on that just as on legal currency, the Bank of Canada alone would issue that credit. No chartered bank would have the right to create a single dollar. The Bank of Canada would create these new credits to the benefit of the country and individual Canadian citizens and not the chartered banks to their own profit. This is what we of the Social Credit party advocate.
It is legalized theft by the chartered banks. This is why there is still misery today. So long as the government does not regain authority over monetary credit, new credits, we will be faced with this difficulty because as soon as we produce something, as soon as we declare a net production we borrow its value the day after. We have to borrow to put it on the market. How ridiculous! Goods are worth the cost of production plus 10 per cent because chartered banks do not lend without interest. This is where the evil lies because our debt which adds up to $67 billion represents only the interest on a capital which we should not have borrowed because it belonged to us in the first place. This is why we have been saying for so long that we must absolutely bring about a separation between these two things, that the public sector must be financed by public capital, by the Bank of Canada, and that the private sector must be financed by the private capital.
The fact is that the public sector these days is financed by private capital. The public sector must necessarily pay the interest charges. There is a total change of economy. Within a single economy we do not have the right to charge interest because this would unleash a galloping inflation, but between two different economies one can charge interest and that is why the chartered banks charge interest to the federal government. They charge interest on something which belonged to the federal government and which the federal government should have injected in the financial circuit. There lies the secret. It is not as complicated as it may seem. There are some people for whom money represents a mystery. They make a mystery out of it but it is not so at all. I think that as long as we fail to get back to reasonable ways of doing things we will encounter problems in bolstering the dollar. It just will be impossible to do it.
It will be still more difficult to pay our national debt because we should keep in mind that we have both a public and a private debt. Our federal debt amounts to $67 billion; we should add to that the $28 billion I already mentioned if we want to go as for as the end of 1979, which will amount to $95 billion at the end of 1979. There are also provincial debts which amount to $16,825 billion, consumer credit which represents $25 billion, corporation credit which totals $31 billion and mortgages which stand at $13 billion, which adds up to a total national debt of $152,825 billion.
Those figures do not include the debt of all Canadian municipalities. The federal deficit alone increases at the rate of $13,700 per minute-1 shall come to that later-$222,000 per hour, $20 million per day. Right now the average debt per capita in Canada, including people from all categories, children, and senior citizens, amounts to $6,900. You should add to this the interests on the $28 billion, and the debt is going to go up from $6,800 to close to $7,500 per capita, and $27,600 per family.
Interests we have to pay on the Canadian debt amount to $6.5 billion a year, on provincial debts $1,228,225,000, on consumer credit $2.5 billion, on finance company loans to corporations $3.1 billion, on mortgages $1.5 billion. In the end, total interests are in the order of $14,628,225,000. This means Canadians will be paying $1,693,000 a minute on the total debt, or $40,633,944 a day. In 1978 the interests on the total debt will be $665 per capita, and with the $28 billion they will be $1,000 per capita. I said earlier we were the most heavily taxed and most interest burdened nation in the world, well the figure is $2,660 per household.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read more of that, but I will now turn to the deficit. I simply wanted to give an idea of how far this country is now into debt. We are wrestling with deficits and that fight is not over yet because as long as we do not get out of that "gimmick" there is no hope. We do not control our credit, we control nothing here. Our lives are

October 19, 1978

controlled by financial circles and chartered banks. I blame nobody. Whoever the minister may be, whether he is a Conservative or a Liberal, he will be doing the same thing under that "gimmick". They can do no better. The "gimmick" has to be changed. Today we are wrestling with large deficits, including the balance of payments deficit. Where do those balance of payments deficits come from? In the first place there is the merchandise trade. We export too much raw materials and not enough finished products. When I think we have to import food products, we produce some 40 per cent of our food. Imagine, in a country like Canada, 40 per cent only. When it comes to furniture and other products, it is even worse. All we export abroad is raw materials-our iron, our aluminum, our steel, all this goes abroad then comes back as finished products.
As long as governments do not care for and do not invest in secondary and tertiary industries, as long as they are content with encouraging primary industry, we will have that kind of balance of payments deficits. When it comes to encouraging small businesses, the government may suggest they must have the will to invest. My suggestion is we must give them a break so they can invest.
Here is another contradiction. Canada is practically the country with the highest savings; why then do Canadians who could venture in industry, keep their savings? Because they are afraid. They are afraid of the government. They are afraid of the tax system because if they invest today in industry thereby risking certain amounts of money already invested in fairly safe enterprises to prevent tax people from "swallowing" them up, in two or three years the taxman will eat up their capital. So they prefer to sit on it rather than break their necks.
They will not invest as long as the government does not give premiums to the industry and protect primary and secondary industries. It can very well give subsidies for two and three years and it is done. Small subsidies are paid to encourage them, to save face but after three years, taxes are levied. Tax deductions are granted for a couple years, then three years later . . . Some of my friends followed the suggestion of the government and launched some projects but in the fourth year they were ruined by taxation. The government had taken back its subsidy and at the end of five years, they were bankrupt. Is that to encourage industry? No, Mr. Speaker. Some favours are bestowed on powerful industrialists and on multionation-als. The fact is not always disclosed. It is concealed. Take for example the $40 million paid to the Ford Company. I say that those $40 million would have been more effective in our areas to develop secondary and service industries I can assure you. That is the worker's tax that went there, to a multibillionaire multinational company while they urge our small investors to invest their money and build industries which they will destroy in three or four years. Meanwhile, the government is going to protect the multinationals because they are the ones which put it in power and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the government will have to change its attitude towards industry.
Borrowing Authority Act
They give incentives to encourage small businesses but for one year or two only, which is not enough. They offer them money to pay for two or three years, interests on the money they are going to borrow. Let us be serious! To encourage industry means to support and assist it, as long as it is not profitable. Municipal and other levels of government, as well as big business are allowed to go tax-free for up to 20 years. Why not do the same for small businesses because, next to the farming industry, they are the ones who create steady employment for our workers. I think that point deserves some consideration. From then on, we could have finished products and exportable goods. And what about the milk industry? Even they, do not receive any help. I know some cheese producers who are forced to reduce their export orders by 50 per cent because they cannot obtain the milk they need to to meet the demand. What a joke! Milk producers who exceed their quota are fined.
I have seen some milk producers pay a $2,000 fine in a month because they had gone beyond their quota, yet there is a cheese producer desperate for milk which he cannot get and because of that his contracts are cancelled. This is what is called encouraging exportation. No wonder our balance of payment is showing a deficit. During this time, we import foreign cheese. Our milk goes down the drain and we cannot produce cheese. We see such utterly disgusting and revolting things in Canada that I wonder why the government does not react, why it does not take action to put an end to it. And now they come crying to the House, saying: "There is a deficit in our balance of payment". But they are not doing anything to boost exports in order to balance our payments.
I was referring earlier to individuals who would have risk capital to invest. It will be noted that in the province of Quebec-I have not been in other provinces-large investments-investments dealers surely know that-are safe. Municipal and school board debentures are safe investments. But people will not risk money in business or industrial ventures because they know their investments would not be guaranteed. Those are not safe investments. They witness so many bankruptcies, I do not blame them and I tell them: You are right!
Let us wait until such time as we have sensible laws that can protect us, because I took a chance myself and lost money on some industries, but never again. Yet I was confident. But income tax has ruined industry. I suppose that all other private investors are like that. They go for what is safe. Anyone who owns a business, who runs it day by day and who is careful will wait for the tax inspectors and watch them so that they will not steal too much from him. Some people think that tax inspectors will only try to catch cheats in business or industry.
I can tell you that I personally won a battle against such inspectors, because I was not the one who cheated, they were. And they thought they would get me. That is what prompts

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
people to say: Well, sometimes you win, sometimes you lose. It will always be like that as long as people have such a mentality, as long as they are not honest enough to recognize the efforts made by some for society and their fellow citizens, in order to create employment. Some civil servants think that they are paid to collect taxes.
When after five years of easy-going management someone comes to a small businessman for a check and he must show the receipts for a five-year period. Imagine! That is the end and the only solution left to him is to shut down his shop and clear out his stock. This is what happens.
Mr. Speaker, once again we do not ask ourselves why private investment is lagging in Canada. As far as interests are concerned, that is another problem. We are told that the Bank of Canada and the other banks increase interest rates to avoid a flight of capital out of the country. Imagine! But they do not realize that by trying to do so they paralyse the whole market.
Money is too expensive, industries cannot operate any more, neither can businesses; they paralyse everything by trying to prevent capital from flying out of the country. I think it would be much better, as I said earlier, to throw the dice, to prevent that flight of capital, to help protect the capital invested in Canada, and so investors will not think about investing elsewhere. Let us not be afraid. They invest abroad, because they are afraid to see the government take what they have left. That is why they take their money out of the country. When the government passes legislation to protect that capital, I think we shall begin to reduce our deficits.
Once again, I should like to invite the government to separate both sectors, namely the public and the private sectors, and to have the public sector financed by public capital, by national revenue and the private sector financed by private capital.
Today I can understand why the Prime Minister (Mr Trudeau) says that there are only two ways of financing a country, taxes and income taxes. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker! I was so surprised to hear that, it floored me. Only two ways, yet we know that Canada is a producing country, but what happens to its products? I think we should start using production like a father does with his household, and if at year end there is not enough, then you resort to taxes, if there is a deficit, but before that you have to use the product that you have.
And what is that product? Well, it is the revenue generated by each year's new production that the government, through the Bank of Canada, must transform into money, and give to the people. Really! If the country has produced 45 billion, well you have to start using that before taxing everyone for 45 billion. That is where I understand the Prime Minister's statement. He does not give a hoot about revenue. He ignores it, that belongs to the chartered banks. We are going to have to claim our goods and tell the Bank of Canada: Now, that
new production, you are going to create it, then deposit it, and register it in the books of the Bank of Canada. What is it going to be used for? For Canadian expenditures. The federal government, instead of borrowing as it does, is going to have $45 billion on hand, and if the provinces need it, they are also part of the national economy and they are going to borrow there. If they need $50 million, they will get it interest free, of course. This is an economic principle whereby if you use money within the same economy you do not even have the right to charge interest because that is going to create galloping inflation. But why are governments borrowing today? Because they have given up the goods of the people, and then they are force to borrow them and put them on the market. That is all. It is clear.
Well, listen to what an economist has to say:
Another economist looked into that problem of government financing and came to the conclusion that Social Crediters discovered long ago, namely financing public capital with new interest free credit.
Interest free, of course. Take a father within his household economy. When he goes and gets $200 from his bank account, does he think about paying interest into his own account? No, it is within the same economy. He would be making a mistake if he paid interest to himself. For a country, it is the same thing; the economy is much larger, that is all. It is the same thing. If the money is there at the Bank of Canada, it belongs to the country, the nation. The government has no business paying interest to itself if it is required for the nation. But they should be the ones and the only ones to have the right to create money, not chartered banks. All chartered banks today think they have the right to monetize the production of the people of Canada by multiplying their assets by 16; they take over the production of the people of Canada for personal purposes- chartered banks are private industries. I do not blame them for that.
When we can make people understand that that system must be corrected, chartered banks will become like caisses populaires. Caisses Populaires are doing very well, as well as chartered banks, but what is straining chartered banks today is that they have to create so much because they have to finance the public sector. But should the public sector ever manage to finance itself through the Bank of Canada, chartered banks will have only the private sector left, and that will be enough.
Everything will work out and the Canadian people will be able to benefit from the credit of their country. This is not the case now as only banks and trusts benefit from Canadian revenue. About ten big companies benefit from the national credit and everyone else is taxed. When the worker produces for a value of $1,000, for instance, he is taxed for $1,000. This has been said by an economist. This theory is explained in a volume entitled "The Challenge of Abundance", by Mr. Robert Thoebald, which can be found in the Library of Parliament. This is what Mr. Thoebald says in this regard:

October 19, 1978

A government may use three methods to obtain the funds required to meet its commitments. First of all, it can tax-
-and this government knows what it means to tax, like all its predecessors.
First of all, it can tax the citizens and the institutions to gain control over their money. Second, it can borrow the money from the people and the institutions and pay interest on the sums borrowed. Third, it can simply create the money and use the funds generated to make its purchases.
This is what I was saying earlier, and it is very simple. You simply have to follow up on Mackenzie King, who ordered that in future all legal tender would be controlled exclusively by the Bank of Canada, and add that the same would apply to monetary credit. That is all you would have to do to set the whole thing straight. Chartered banks would remain and have the same function; they would remain commercial banks, but Canada would be in a much better situation and Canadians would stop having the product of their work stolen each year, and I say "stolen" because I believe that this is a national theft that benefits chartered banks. As long as this is not done, Mr. Speaker, we will continue to complain about deficits and borrow to pay off the interests, and ten years from now, we will not even be able to borrow to pay off these interests.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining this debate on the motion put forth by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) for the additional borrowing authority the government is seeking I should like first to make reference to some of the points made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), the financial critic for the official opposition and presumably the senior financial spokesman for the Conservative party. Some of the points he made were a little surprising to me bearing in mind the importance of the position the hon. member for York-Simcoe occupies. The nation is looking at the official opposition rather carefully this week. Hon. members on that side of the House are gleeful as a result of some developments of a very temporary nature a few days ago; people are looking more closely at their senior spokesman and I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe stands out as their spokesman on matters related to finance.
The hon. member knows very well that the additional authority sought through this bill is not intended to cover additional spending by the government. In fact, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) have repeated over and over again since the declaration of last August, it is the intention of the government to reduce substantially expenditures over the years ahead. The hon. member knows this. He knows authority is being obtained now to cover the government's needs not only for the balance of the present fiscal year but for the next fiscal year so as to avoid our having to come back to parliament time and time again for the necessary legislation if we are to meet the expenditures which he himself, along with other members of the finance committee, examined
Borrowing Authority Act
in detail when the estimates were before the committee last spring and supported there. If expenditures are made, they have to be paid for. That is the purpose of this authority. It is of a routine nature. It is the kind of thing which must be brought before parliament from time to time to make sure that sufficient funds are on hand to meet commitments.
The hon. member referred to briefcases and to washrooms, presumably in the course of what he considered to be mature and deliberate comments. He gave us some figures which are of small significance in relation to total government expenditures. I am not sure why he mentioned briefcases; they are used, I suppose, by a large number of the 300,000 civil servants engaged in government and agency work. But the hon. member did not refer to the full four billion or five billion which he and his leader have recommended should be spent and added to the country's deficit in the course of the recent election campaign. Add up all the goodies the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), supported by the hon. member for York-Simcoe and others across the way, indicated they would hand out if they formed the government of this country and one would be coming forward with a bill seeking authority to borrow not the amount mentioned in this measure but $4 billion or $5 billion more.

speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
I perused some of the literature put out by the party opposite, full of doom and gloom and references to the terrible situation we are in, but I do not recall the cost of those promises being shown as an addition to the deficit which we all agree is already too high and must be reduced. The attitude was: If you buy these goodies there is a price tag but we will tell you what it is later on. We believe the people should be told about the price tab now and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, we shall make a point of doing so.
The official critic for the Conservative party indicated we were fiddling around in foreign markets borrowing money and gave the impression that this was a very strange thing to do; I think he said only two countries had made such loans before. The point he did not bring out was that the Deutschmark loan this government made was taken out at a rate of 5 per cent. He did not mention that for the obvious reason that it was a darned good deal; it is not in the interests of members of that party to indicate to the public that anything done by this government is in the interests of the Canadian people. That loan was a good deal.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: A good deal of money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The hon. member also gave the impression that all the money that was being borrowed was being frittered away on day to day expenditures, that the government was borrowing these great amounts of money just to pay salaries and current expenses. He made no reference to the fact that part of the government expenditures in this two-year period is being devoted to a number of major capital projects which will bring long-term benefits. Large amounts of money are being invested in tar sands development. Money is being invested

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
through CMHC in houses for senior citizens, co-operative housing and other types of housing projects involving direct financing.
Nor did he mention many other areas where capital expenditures rather than current spending is involved, among them, transfers to the provinces involving capital programs such as the building of hospitals and other facilities under shared costs arrangements with the federal government.
It is obvious we have been obliged to use some long-term funds to deal with the U.S. exchange problem, again, as the Minister of Finance has said so often, to ensure an orderly market. The hon. member made a great point of emphasizing that we were applying now for money for the next fiscal year. Mr. Speaker, the bill is presented in this form so that no more parliamentary time will be taken up than is necessary and we can get on with more positive things which need to be done. The funds will not be used until actually needed, but the authority will be there.
I would like to refer again to the comments of the hon. member for York-Simcoe who ridiculed the fact that the Prime Minister objected to comments made by the Leader of the Opposition when, in his lead speech in the throne speech debate, the Leader of the Opposition said that Canada had dropped to seventh place among the world's richest nations. The Prime Minister asked him to specify which countries were involved, but no specifics were given. The Prime Minister referred to some small countries which indeed might be ahead in terms of the riches that they have enjoyed in recent years.
When the hon. member for York-Simcoe went into that subject this afternoon, I called across the floor from where I was sitting and asked him to specify the countries he was talking about, if we are in seventh place. He did so, and I will repeat them because I want to discuss those countries and our position among them. The hon. member mentioned West Germany, Belgium, Norway, Sweden, the U.S.A., Denmark and Switzerland. He said that Canada fell behind all those countries, again conveying the notion to the public at large that Canada is in a much worse position than any of those seven countries and that we have fallen behind them.
Let us look at some of the factors involved with which I assume it would be deemed fair to deal in considering where we stand as far as economic progress in concerned. Let us talk about job-creation. I may be repeating some of the information already put on the record by the Prime Minister, but it must be done because the average Canadian is not getting this information through the media or from members of the opposition, whose plan has been for a year or more, and certainly will be for the next six months, to put before people the ideas that they are in a doom and gloom position. They will not mention any positive facts. It will be up to us to put this information forward over and over again.
Let us talk about job creation, which is a very important matter in any country which considers itself to be doing reasonably well. From 1973 to 1977 Canada outpaced the

U.S.A. and the OECD nations. We were three percentage points ahead of the United States and eight percentage points ahead of the OECD countries.
One of the countries referred to by the financial critic of the official opposition-I am not picking these countries out, he picked them out and I am merely making a comparison-was West Germany. From 1974 to 1977 job creation in West Germany went down 4.1 per cent. In the same period job creation in Switzerland went down 10 per cent. Those are two of the countries the hon. member for York-Simcoe indicated were ahead of Canada in terms of over-all economic progress.
There were 10,635,000 job holders in Canada as of the end of September, 375,000 more than in August of last year. On a seasonally adjusted basis some 279,000 new jobs were created in Canada in the first eight months of 1978. From 1950 to 1976 the labour force here grew at an annual rate of 2.7 per cent. Hon. members opposite laugh. They should be hiding their heads in shame because they are not telling people about these figures. The U.S. rate was less than half our 2.7 per cent rate; it was 1.3 per cent. Hon. members opposite do not like to hear this because it goes against what they are trying to shove down the throats of Canadians.

Order, please. Before giving the floor to the honourable member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) I should like to make a brief reference to the action by the Chair earlier in the day in respect of the amendment put forward by the honourable member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). The Chair reserved the decision on that amendment at that time and simply set it aside. There was no argument raised at that time and the Chair indicated it would be held aside. No point of order had been raised on the matter and the Chair was not advised of any procedural argument that was to be raised.
However, I think it is the duty of the Chair, particularly on second reading amendments, to be on the alert and to advise the House if, in the opinion of the Chair, there is any serious procedural difficulty. Therefore, we examined the contents of the amendment as well as some precedents, notably one from 1970 concerning a ruling of my distinguished predecessor in respect of an amendment put forward at that time by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) on a grain bill. I must confess to some misgivings about the entire practice of reasoned amendments at second reading.
I have looked at the British practice, as I think most hon. members have, and found it to be much more generous than ours. In the British practice it is quite acceptable to attach to a second reading vote a motion which is by way of an amendment to the second reading motion, which seems to be nothing more than an expression of the reason for voting against the motion. We have taken a much tighter line in Canadian

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
practice but, to my regret, not strong enough, because I still think that frequently in our past practice we have permitted this very kind of declaration. Certainly on the occasion of the 1970 precedent which I examined this afternoon we permitted a statement which was really a declaration that the bill somehow offended or was repugnant in principle to members of the House and to some residents of Canada and that the House declined to give second reading to the bill.
If it was permissible at that time in our practice to do that, certainly it must be permissible to do what the hon. member for York-Simcoe has done in this amendment because he introduces at least a new principle which is contrary to that of the bill, that is, the principle of granting borrowing power for future years on the basis of which he says the House declines to give second reading at this time.
I still think that at some time we should select one of these practices, and I am sure that at some time in the future a good example will be chosen and a point of order will be raised which will compel me or a future Speaker to examine all of these so-called reasoned amendments at second reading and find out which ones really are expanded negatives and which ones in fact introduce a statement of a principle declaratory of some principle contrary to the principle of a bill, or whatever the appropriate language is.
In any case, having briefly examined the precedent on this particular occasion, I looked at the amendment that was put forward and I found I really could not single this one out in the light of other precedents. Perhaps the argument will have to come at some future time. Therefore, on the face of it and in the light of the 1970 precedent of Mr. Lamoureux to which I have referred, it seems clear to me that this amendment is in order and should stand on procedural ground.

Mr. Speaker, before I commence the main part of my speech tonight I should like to mention a few things. I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) as he presented a significant point of view. I suggest his point of view is debatable on philosophical grounds; he suggested more government intervention. Perhaps he does not realize the underground economy is already in place. At the present time much is being written about that in the United States, where it is estimated that something like 10 per cent to 15 per cent of the GNP belongs to the underground economy which does not surface in the tax system because of people working part time as well as drawing unemployment benefits. Their employers allow this because they can be paid less. This should be taken into account when we talk about more government intervention.
Agriculture always has been the Achilles heel of the Soviet Union and its economy. Under Mr. Khrushchev a peasant was allowed an acre of land to grow his own produce for the purpose of sale. It was reduced to a half an acre of land because it was felt that having an acre of land was against the philosophy of the Soviets. Eventually it was found that the workers of half-acre parcels quit producing, and Mr. Brezhnev has been given credit for changing the half acre allotment to an acre once again. It is estimated that an acre is roughly 44 times as productive as state farms. More government intervention brings with it a whole train of intervention which we do not always think about.
During a recent airplane trip, I had occasion to speak with a missionary who had lived in South America for 25 years. He had interesting veiwpoints about inflation. I asked him how ordinary people lived in high inflation countries. He said that naturally they did not have very much money, and that they spent it each week to buy food and to pay for shelter. Thus, inflation did not affect them in a sense.
Then we must consider the wealthy, which make up a small proportion who protect themselves by the purchase of gold through the establishment of estates, and so on. I asked how the average individual could protect himself against the ravages of inflation. What he told me was very interesting. He suggested that they might buy a bicycle because not only could they use it but its value would increase as inflation increased.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge also referred to multinational corporations. There is substantial evidence that the influence brought to bear by these corporations around the world is decreasing. Third world countries are establishing their own multinational corporations and companies but the climate for these corporations is not as good as it has been. I think these multinationals have had their day and their influence is less of a factor at the present time.
Borrowing Authority Act
Let me say a word about savings, which are necessarily tied in with these borrowings. It is interesting to note that the present older generation is now saving money. An individual who works in the income tax field told me that he prepares the income tax returns for some 30 people, and he suggests that nearly all of them are saving money, though few of them have assets other than a house and an old age pension. These are thrifty and frugal people. The people who are aware of what is happening to the economy are likely to save as apparently those people have been able to do.
Furthermore, what is happening as a result of more and more intervention in the lives of individuals by governments of the day? Nearly every merchant, baker and butcher say that the consumer affairs people give them a bad time. One individual wondered whether it was worth operating his own business in view of the fact that many civil servants were making twice as much as he was able to make. Many of these people in small businesses are leaving business and joining the civil service because they are much better off. We have reached the stage in this sort of Ralph Nader society where everyone who makes a mousetrap or performs a service is of lesser importance, and certainly worse off financially, than those who police the making of the product or the provision of the service. The suggestion is that everyone who makes a mousetrap or performs a service is somehow ripping off the public. Those are a few of the thoughts I wanted to put on the record for the benefit of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge.
Let me now turn to Bill C-7 which is, in effect, a $7 billion supplementary borrowing authority for the remainder of the current fiscal year, and authority for borrowing $10 billion for the year 1980. Imagine borrowing money for 1980 with more than a few months still remaining in this year. Since the beginning of the fiscal year 1978 the government has sought borrowing authority to a total of $38 billion. It has sought this authority in four different bills. First there was Bill C-45 for $7 billion, then there was Bill C-ll for $9 billion, followed by Bill C-31 for $5 billion, and now Bill C-7 for $17 billion.
At March 31, 1977, the unmatured debt of the Canadian government totalled $42.5 billion. If all the borrowing authority was used, by 1980 the unmatured debt would exceed $80 billion, some 100 per cent above the 1977 level. In fact, in three years we will have doubled the debt.
If we are to go by the past experience of this government it will likely seek further borrowing authority for 1980 even though the department might like to do so without coming for that authority to parliament. The request in Bill C-7 for $7 billion in borrowing authority represents the third time the borrowing ceiling has been raised for the present fiscal year. How can the experts in the minister's department be so wrong as to be required to come to the House of Commons three times to increase the borrowing ceiling?
The minister requested the $9 billion increase in Bill C-ll with the claim that it would cover the remaining cash requirements for 1978 and the cash requirements well into the new
286

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
fiscal year. In March of this year the minister came back with Bill C-31 saying the new ceiling would provide the government with sufficient borrowing power to meet all the cash requirements for the 1978-79 fiscal year. Now he wants another $7 billion to cover foreign borrowing, the Canada Savings Bonds issue and other contingencies.
Let me turn now to the foreign exchange problem. It is obvious we are in a bad way in this regard. It is now realized that had there been no foreign exchange borrowing by the government our foreign exchange reserves would have been at zero. We are rapidly becoming as badly off as the British. Soon we will be joining those nations which lop all the zeroes off their currency. It seems the minister has to go to the New York market for a $750 million bond issue. I understand this issue commenced this morning. This bond issue is the third federal foreign currency bond issue this year. In April there was a $750 million issue in the United States. In May there was a German Deutschmark issue equivalent to $706 million in United States currency. In a seven-month period the Government of Canada will have issued $2.2 billion in foreign currency bonds.
Interest must be paid on these bond issues or borrowings just as it has to be paid on a line of credit with U.S. banks. All of this adds to the deficit of Canada's balance of payments. This is obviously going to mean some $200 million extra in interest payments. These additional interest payments are required at the very time when there is a deficit in the interest and dividends account, and it is growing by leaps and bounds.
I am reminded of the fact that some years ago a New York banker suggested to Canadians that when they borrow they should at least be friendly with their bankers. I think the reason the minister is here tonight is to obtain the agreement of parliament in respect of these borrowings.
In the first half of this year the deficit on interest dividend payments was $1.7 billion, up 17 per cent from a comparable period in 1977, and 80 per cent greater than the deficit in the first half of 1976. Just this year alone the interest on the federal issue will raise the interest and dividend deficit by a full 5 per cent.
One could ask why the minister needs $10 billion in borrowing authority for 1980, particularly when we are a long way, in a parliamentary sense, from the end of March. Perhaps the minister feels like the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) when he complained about the breakfast served at the world hunger seminar, that this is "just the same old buns , as the minister said. He said, "I thought it was going to be like the MP's breakfast in Ottawa; we get in the cafeteria there and you get to pick out your scrambled eggs or whatever you want". The minister told a Washington audience how wealthy Canadians are despite the doom and gloom about the economy. He said, "I walk up the driveways and I see two cars in the garage, ranch-type houses, so much money in the credit union, just back from a trip to Europe or some other place". If we are so wealthy why do we have to go down to Washington every three months to borrow money?

Obviously inflation is a monetary phenomenon. There can be no inflation in a bartering economy, when in fact goods and services bear a relationship to the money supply and the costs increase proportionately. There is no doubt that deficit financing is contributing to the inflationary process that has been taking place.
What has the situation been in respect of financing requirements in the last decade? From 1966 to 1968 we experienced deficit financing to the extent of $2,578 million. In 1972-74 we required $3,271 million, and in 1975-76 we required $14,334 million. Now we have this enormous rise in deficits in the last two years. In fact, it is estimated that the deficit for 1977-78 will be increased by some $10 billion. If one can believe the statistics that are available it will be consideraby more- perhaps as high as $16 billion. The estimate for 1978 to 1979, on the best authority I have, is that it will be somewhere between $11 billion and $12 billion. The government has had a very bad habit of budgeting for a deficit considerably smaller than it ends up with. In the 1972-74 period over $2 billion of the $3 billion was amortized or monetized by the Bank of Canada, or 66 per cent of the requirements in that period. Obviously those were the days of minority government, one of the factors that set off the inflationary cycle.
There has recently been a steady progression required by the Bank of Canada as a percentage of net financing required. What stands out clearly-and this is a crucial point-is the inability or the unwillingness shown by the Government of Canada in obtaining non-inflationary financing-that is, sales to the non-banking general public-and its increasing reliance on the printing presses.
If credit demands rise faster than money supply, the competition for funds causes interest rates to rise, thus rationing out the weakest borrowers, that is, those unwilling or unable to pay the higher cost of funds. We see it happening already as the Bank of Canada raises the rate. If, however, at this stage the central bank prefers to keep interest rates from rising too quickly, either because it fears derailing the ongoing expansion or because, in its wisdom, it feels that interest rates are high enough, then it is forced to monetize the increasing credit demands.
This is exactly what happened in that ill-fated period of 1972-74 when the treasury and/or the central bank feared bidding up funds too aggressively, so as to place the entire government loan with the investing public, with the result that the Bank of Canada was forced to take up as much as 66 per cent of the government's net financing requirements. The enormous appetite of the public sector acts as a drag to the economy by crowding out the private sector; caught in this dilemma, the Bank of Canada comes to the rescue and purchases or monetizes government debt.
In the subsequent 1975-77 period, as the Canadian economy moved into a severe growth recession and private sector credit demands abated, the government was able to place an increasing proportion of financing requirement directly with the
October 19, 1978

private saver. In those years it was a lot less. The 1975-77 period only required a total financing of some $7 billion. We are faced in two years with an enormous deficit of $20 billion which is projected for this year and next.
We have long been used, Mr. Speaker, to a foreign exchange deficit. So long as the Canadian dollar remains stable, it can be handled easily enough, particularly when foreigners have confidence in our economy and the stability of our political situation. But this has been clouded by the province of Quebec and the possibilities of serious disruption of our ability to pay our debts.
What are people who know saying about our Canada Savings Bonds? People are looking at them closely and they are described by many as a "con game". At the end of the year there will be on a $1,000 bond $85, $90 or $95 interest more or less. But in buying power this represents less money than the buyer had at the start. Furthermore, the $85 interest will be taxed at his marginal rate of income tax. In effect, a loss is guaranteed on these bonds. There is not the slightest chance of making a profit as long as inflation continues.
We distinctly hear asked the question: How low can the dollar go? It is said we are being locked into a collapsing currency. Our deficit financing has grown until there is obviously no bottom to the Canadian dollar. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) says that a depressed dollar is good for exports. But it is also inflationary because everything coming into this country from the United States is going to cost 15 per cent more than it did a year ago. We have depreciated in the past year some 30 per cent more or less against the Japanese yen, yet the price of a bushel of buckwheat for the western farmer, a product destined for Japan, is the same price this year as last-$4.75 a bushel. 1 will not use the metric system in describing the price in tonnes-a system bitterly resented by the western farmers.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has consistently overstated the growth rate. It has always been, he states, 5 per cent or 5.5 per cent, but it has not measured up to this during his time in that portfolio. Other people whose opinions and judgments are valued and considered have always been much less optimistic than the Minister of Finance.
Why does the minister want this borrowing authority at this moment, particularly for 1980? Does he expect a sudden run on the dollar? Perhaps he is concerned about the three-year old dividend controls which expired last week. No one knows what the impact of unmatured dividend flows will be on the shaky Canadian dollar which is now trading at a 45-year low against the U.S. dollar. This outflow, even if it is minimal, will not help our dollar. Some would suggest this outflow could be as high as $1 billion over a short period or up to $2 billion over a longer period. All in all, the situation for the Canadian economy is very clouded. The minister could well enlighten us a great deal more as to why he wants these enormous borrowings; indeed, we need an explanation.
I will close with these remarks, Mr. Speaker, but I look forward with interest to finding out from the minister why he needs to have the ceiling raised so far ahead. Is it because an
Borrowing Authority Act
election must come within a year? Is it that he does not want to be embarrassed at election time by a run on the Canadian dollar?

Mr. Speaker, once again we have a government bill to provide supplementary borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1978-79. It seems that all we do here is discuss bills to provide for more borrowing. If we are not borrowing more money it seems we are spending more money or printing more money, which is a clear indication that the government does not know what it is doing and does not know the first thing about running this country.
This all started ten years ago when the rules of this House were changed to reduce the number of votes. There is no proper examination of the departmental estimates by parliament; there is no control over government spending. This has been pointed out year after year by the Auditor General. Even he cannot find out where the money is going.
Having listened to the comments from the government benches today I suggest that hon. members opposite should read the Auditor General's reports to find out what is going on in the country. The government would have us believe that everything is beautiful, our accounts are in good order and there is no need to appoint a Comptroller General at an initial cost of $6 million per year. The government seems to be proud of borrowing money all the time, but that is nothing to brag about. A government or a business cannot be run by borrowing money all the time. It is a clear indication that the government does not know what it is doing.
I should like to put on the record some remarks attributed to the Comptroller General in an article in the Winnipeg Free Press on September 29, 1978, datelined Edmonton:
The federal government's system of financial planning and control is unsuitable for the current period of economic restraint, the Comptroller General of Canada said Thursday.
Harry Rogers said in a speech to the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants that the system evolved in a period of rapid expansion of government activities.
"Without changes in these financial and manpower planning and control systems, the government will be severely limited in its ability to implement changes in its priorities."
It is odd that tonight the parliamentary secretary, who is supposed to be an accountant, did not comment on the matters raised by the Comptroller General. He informed us that this borrowing has something to do with reducing spending in the years ahead. The government has been in office for the last 15 years and it appears now that they are getting on to this so-called restraint and reduction of spending because of the latest opinion polls. It is not in them to have a really proper accounting system, to reduce spending or to see that our tax dollars are spent properly.
We are also informed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and his Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Martin) that this bill is a routine matter. He stated that we voted for this

When I was at home in my riding during the recess, I was learning about more borrowing by reading the newspaper. I was not called back here to vote for any of this borrowing.
