Just in passing, there was another comment made about the great progress in housing and it was said that housing starts are up again. There are 72,000 new homes in this country today that remain empty. That is a dismal record for a country like Canada. People simply cannot afford to get into these homes. We recommended a mortgage deductibility plan that has been in effect in the United States for 40 years. It has been very successful. It has been in effect in Great Britain for many years and it has been very successful there. We want to implement a plan like this in Canada to help people buy homes. In return all we receive is criticism from the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and all the rest of them. All they have is a lot of negative criticism to offer.
I was also interested in the comments expressed by the financial critic of the New Democratic Party tonight. He criticized our party's financial critic. He listed a lot of small items that could be curtailed. However, there is no NDP member in the House tonight to listen to my comments. That is typical.
The comments of the New Democratic Party's financial critic seem to be right in step with this government. He said, "If the government spends more, the private sector will also spend more". That is a great theory. I have some evidence that will shatter that comment.
We had a change of government in Manitoba a year ago and I will give some statistics to show what is happening there. Expenditures are being curtailed. Not only that, the government is bringing in proper management and eliminating waste. Construction has experienced the greatest gain in Manitoba this year in the commercial sector. It is up a whopping 3,542 per cent from a mere $1 million worth last year when we had an NDP socialist government in Manitoba. We are up $38.4 million in 1978 so far.
After a loss of 6,000 jobs in the manufacturing sector under the NDP government, an increase in excess of 8,000 jobs in the past year has been evidenced. Expenditures are being curtailed. The private sector has faith in responsible government and as a result they are spending more. That is the evidence. In Manitoba building permits are up 69 per cent over 1977, when there was a New Democratic Party government in power which had all spending out of control. By having a responsible government eliminating waste and mismanagement, the private sector has expressed its faith in that government, and they will now invest in that province. That discounts the argument of the critic of the NDP.
Another example of what is happening in Manitoba by bringing in proper management and eliminating waste concerns the St. Boniface General Hospital in Winnipeg. This

hospital has been able to reduce its operating expenditures for this year by $3,700,000. This has been accomplished as a result of the president of the hospital working with the staff to set up a program of eliminating wasteful things and bringing in more efficient management. This hospital is still maintaining proper quality patient care. The quality of care for the patients is not being reduced. This is one hospital, one institution. The New Democratic Party critic said that we are talking about peanuts, small amounts. However, this is a $3,700,000 saving at one hospital. Mr. Quaglia, the president of the hospital, has listed in a document how they accomplished it. It shows that it can be done. I would like to see all of the policies and programs that were adopted at this particular hospital adopted in all of the government departments in Ottawa. We are talking about reducing taxes by $2 billion. We could probably reduce them by $10 billion if we implemented a program such as the one in existence at the St. Boniface General Hospital in Winnipeg.
The parliamentary secretary accused Conservative candidates in the by-elections of using false and misleading information and said that all our statistical information is wrong. I challenge that statement, Mr. Speaker. I commented on this last Monday night. Canada's Prime Minister used a lot of selective statistical information in his speech on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. This was picked up by the news media and the Prime Minister has been challenged.
I have not heard the Liberal party challenging the statements made by Mr. Don McGillivray of Southam News. One of the things he had to say is as follows:
Most of Trudeau's statistics used 1970 as the "base year" or starting point. He was elaborately casual about it, saying that any other year would do as well. But when one looks at the resulting members, it is clear that 1970 was well chosen. It is an example of "the before-and-after trick" described in Darrell Huffs 1954 classic, "How to Lie with Statistics".
One can be sure that the Liberal party would dig up a document like that to help them along. Mr. McGillivray goes on to say:
If you compare your income this year with the one when you were out of a job and living on unemployment insurance, you have made fantastic gains. But if you compare it with the year you won the lottery, you have slipped badly.
Nineteen seventy happened to be a recession year in Canada. It was the lowest point for housing starts, for example, in the past 10 years. Only 191,000 units were started.
So when Trudeau claims a 25 per cent gain in housing starts he is measuring against a bad year. If you move the base year to 1971 when 233,000 houses were started, the gain shrinks to 5 per cent.
The Prime Minister should be completely and totally responsible and should not be using a bunch of tricky statistics.
This example of how this government operates is a clear indication that you cannot really trust them. This is why everybody is so suspicious. Look at the things which they allow to go on and how they allow taxpayers' money to be squandered. I have one other example to give. The New Democratic Party probably will not like this because it concerns $200,000 of the taxpayers' money. I have an article entitled "Why do the Gals Take so Long", and it reads:
October 19, 1978

The mandarins in Ottawa decided that an urgent question of great public concern, "how long do people spend in public washrooms", had to be settled. To that end they allotted in the neighbourhood of $200,000 to have this nagging question answered.
You will be heartened to know the results. By depositing themselves in the washrooms of Ottawa's National Arts Centre during intermission, recording arrival rates, duration and frequency of toilet traffic, researchers flushed out the fact that a man spends an average of 41 seconds at a urinal, while a woman spends 75 seconds using the cubicle.
There is a classic example. I guess I should not have raised that becaue it involves only $200,000 of the taxpayers' money and I realize it is not a large amount.
One also questions the credibility of the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). His word does not mean anything. On Wednesday, August 13, 1969, the Prime Minister, at a major press conference over national television, talked to the Canadian people about inflation and the country's financial future. He said this:
We would be on the way to financial disaster if nothing were done to bring spending under control. To spend vast sums on welfare, education, and other progams while allowing inflation to continue would merely place hundreds of thousands of Canadians on a treadmill they could not escape.
I never read more meaningless words in my life. He never meant one word of it. The Prime Minister also committed his government to a substantial cut in the federal public service. What has happened since August 13, 1969? Government spending has increased by over $34 billion, some 230 per cent. We now hear the parliamentary secretary trying to brush all this under the rug.
Here is something else that is driving Canadian taxpayers and the official opposition up the wall in connection with these phony programs. Although we are not opposed to sound foreign aid programs which will help our trade picture, some of them are very questionable. I quote from an excellent editorial in the Toronto Sun of October 8:
Our federal government has got to be crazy. Out of its maple syrup mind. Either that or criminally negligent. Or, horrors, both!
Here the damned country is falling apart, we're in the pits economically, and Trudeau's pledge a couple of months back (at the Bonn economic summit) of a 5 per cent growth rate has crumbled. Now Canada will be lucky if it hits 3 per cent growth.
Two years ago our dollar was worth nearly 5 per cent more than the American. Today it is worth 20 per cent less. And still fading. This year the feds have borrowed some $5 billion in futile, desperate attempts to shore up the slipping dollar. It is said to cost Canada $85,000 a day merely to keep a line of credit open. That's $85,000 a day with no tangible returns!
It sounds incredible, but it may not be beyond Trudeau's talents to bankrupt Canada.
And now the crazy part: In the midst of this chaos Canada has just borrowed $1.2 billion in order to lend it to Algeria! Unbelievable. Borrowing and paying interest in order to lend to Algeria! See what we mean when we suggest the government is nuts? Or wicked ...
Watinell is the magic hold Algeria holds over the Trudeau government anyway? One of the world's more repressive regimes, it aids and protects terrorists, it actively tries to subvert neighbouring countries it doesn't like, it tramps on its own citizens, and it is nurtured with Soviet weaponry. But it speaks French . .. And Canada borrows to lend it dough-probably forgiveable loans (the feds won't tell), which cost us 10 per cent... Yet we pay some 10 per cent interest.
Borrowing Authority Act
It likely costs Canada $300,000 a day in interest to loan Algeria money to buy from Canada, which will be a phony boost to our export statistics. This is called "creative accounting" and any private firm which tried it would be bankrupt or its executives jailed.
I wonder if the parliamentary secretary, who is an accountant, tells this to the firms he represents. I certainly would not want my tax form filled out by his accounting firm. The article continues:
Algeria is one of the biggest recipients of Canadian aid anyway. Now this $1.2 billion bonanza. And Algeria isn't even an ally. It is a "socialist" military dictatorship which shoots, hangs, assassinates or imprisons political opponents. It has 80 per cent illiteracy and no civil liberties. Why is Canada aiding such a regime at the expense of Canadians?
It constitutes a moral and financial outrage and those responsible should be horsewhipped. Or worse ...
That was a classic example. The government suggests that we rubber-stamp all of these bills with billions here, borrow more there and all the rest. Many government members are critical of this side of the House and our successful candidates in the by-election. It is negative criticism which is not warranted. Well, we have a lot of company on our side.
As I mentioned last Monday night, more and more responsible people are studying and analysing how this government has mismanaged our affairs over the years. This is being documented in books such as the one I have here. This is not a series of general statements and opinions; these books contain statistical information.
The book I have here is entitled "The Canadian Economy, Its Problems and Its Potential", published under the auspices of Burns Fry Limited. The author is G. Leigh Skene. I wish to highlight a few of the points it makes:
It is now clear that the explosion in government spending during the past decade has left us with intolerable unemployment, intolerable inflation, and an intolerable burden of taxation. What makes our plight even more serious is that traditional government remedies, over the short term at least, can only exacerbate our problems. More and bigger government deficits-the common political response-would only act to unduly increase the money supply. That in turn would raise unit labour costs as well as other prices. The result then would be an increased volume of imports. Increasing the gap between imports and exports means the export of jobs-
They are being exported on a daily basis. Some figures indicate that up to $18 million a day is leaving, most of it going to the United States, because there is no faith in this government or this country.
And that means lower federal revenues, higher government spending, and more massive deficits.
It goes on to ask:
Do Government Deficits Cause Inflation?
There has been an ongoing controversy in Canada as to whether government deficits cause inflation.
They certainly do. There are a number of chapters on this. There is a chart which shows what is going on in this country. In their wrap-up, they refer to the role of the electorate in avoiding the crisis. I quote:
Perhaps most important of all, none of the reforms detailed in this chapter can come about without an electorate which chooses opportunity over handouts. As long as the voter chooses the candidate who promises more giveaways rather than the one who offers realistic solutions to our problems, there will be no lasting prosperity.

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
I can say without boasting that I have never stood on a platform and said: If you vote for me I will give you something for nothing. This nonsense was started by the Prime Minister in 1972 and a former minister of finance, John Turner, while parading around this country.
Can you imagine the Prime Minister trying to bribe the taxpayers with their own money, saying if you vote for me, there will be lots of goodies. We had an example of that in Winnipeg. He was going to give us a hangar. Now we have a $15 million hangar but they do not know what to do with it. Well, bribery did not work there. The parliamentary secretary is saying that we promised goodies. We did not do any such thing. I again quote:
What is lacking is will and determination. No society every received more than it earned, and this one will not be any exception to the rule. If expectations are high the level of effort must be high to achieve these expectations. If the level of effort is low, then the achievement level will be also. A continuation of the current levels of effort will bring about a very low achievement level.
In this document are a number of excellent recommendations. I will only refer to two. I quote:
Reduce the annual rate of increase in federal spending to 2 per cent to 4 per cent per annum.
Eliminate the federal budget deficit in a four to five year controlled program.
Of course, this is what we have been calling for for many years. We presented a motion on February 2 of this year calling for the strengthening of the committee system. We wanted the government to bring in sunset laws and, through the committee system, to examine every government department to find out exactly what they are doing and implement a program along the lines of that followed in Manitoba. But the New Democratic Party and the Liberal party are not interested at all in curtailing spending or conducting a proper examination of what is going on. The criticism we received was extraordinary.
We talked about a review of the tax system on May 23 of this year. There have been complaints from all over the country about our tax structure and we wanted to set down the proper committees to review that structure and attempt to improve our economic situation by encouraging investors to stay in Canada. Again we encountered blazing criticism from the New Democratic Party and from the Liberals. Now they come here again and say they are going to curtail spending. Those are meaningless words. They are not fooling me for one second.
Some excellent work has been done in the Senate. I should like to refer to a study which was completed earlier this year. It is called "Canada-United States Relations" and I am quoting from volume two which deals with Canada's trading relations with the United States. This is a document compiled by the Senate standing committee on foreign affairs; it should be required reading for all members of parliament and espa-cially for those who sit on the government benches.
I should like to refer to a few of the areas covered in this study. One of them is headed "Deterioration in the Travel Account". We know that this year there is likely to be a $2

billion tourism deficit. We hear from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) that he is holding great meetings, that he is going to cure all our tourism problems and that everyone will be coming to Canada. Those are more meaningless words.
I should like to give hon. members an example of how these matters are really handled. This is what happened in Manitoba during the summer. Northwest Air Lines, which flies from Chicago and Minneapolis to Winnipeg, was in a four-month strike. This meant that 14,000 fewer passengers were carried to northern Manitoba by Transair. A great number of Americans come up each year to fish and hunt in Manitoba but 14,000 fewer came this year; we have these statistics from Transair which picks them up in Winnipeg and takes them to the north.
While the strike was on we asked Air Canada to put on a regular flight to help us with this problem. But the corporation would do nothing about it. I telephoned the President of Air Canada and I wrote to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). Air Canada has the right to fly from Winnipeg to Minneapolis and Chicago. They have had that right for almost a year but will not exercise that franchise. Nor will they give it to anyone else. This is a government airline, Mr. Speaker. Why did they not step in to help us or at least hand the franchise over to Transair so that they could have gone down to Chicago and Minneapolis and brought these 14,000 wealthy Americans up to spend money in northern Manitoba? I would venture to say that 14,000 fewer wealthy Americans getting up to northern Canada this summer cost us untold millions, because they are big spenders. That is an example of the way in which the government and its agencies are helping out with our tourism problem. There is a chapter in this study dealing with the basic cause of this tourism deficit. It goes into great detail.
One of the highlights of the document is the suggestion that Canada is no longer an attractive country in which to invest money because of the fact that the Saskatchewan government nationalized the potash industry in Saskatchewan a number of years ago. The Senate report states:
The nationalization by the Saskatchewan government of the potash industry produced a strong negative reaction from the United States. The United States is heavily dependent upon Saskatchewan as a source for potash; almost 70 per cent of its potash needs came from Canada in 1974.
That was the start of it, Mr. Speaker. A combination of this action by the NDP government in Saskatchewan and the policies of the Liberal government here has given rise to fears among investors that Canada was no longer an attractive country in which to invest.
The Senate committee also dealt with the subject of resource taxation. A number of witnesses were called and they made some extremely interesting comments. The committee set forth its views as follows:
A major problem for the Canadian resource industries and particularly the mining industry in recent years relates to the jurisdictional disputes between the federal and provincial government over the right to tax. The mining industry tax incentives structure was substantially altered in 1971 by changes in federal tax policy which removed some of the advantages which the industry had traditionally enjoyed. The impact of this change was compounded by steps taken within a
October 19, 1978

couple of years by the provinces to tax away the profit generated in the prosperous 1973-74 period which, it is now apparent, was due to cyclical factors.
We are all aware of the potential of the mining industry in Canada. We want to do everything we possibly can to encourage it. Unfortunately, the federal government and some of the provincial governments have treated this industry very badly. The result has been extremely costly for Canada. Further in this document we read:
Mr. Alfred Powis, President of Noranda, termed as "devastating" the over-all impact of the federal government's 1971 tax reform coupled with the punitive taxes and royalties of the provinces which the federal government disallowed as expenses. In terms of competitive position, he said, Canadian taxes were more than double those in parts of the United States.
These are some of the things we wanted to discuss in committee so that we could solve these problems and get Canada going. But no co-operation was forthcoming from the NDP or from the government. The company prepared for the committee, as evidence of this, tables of comparable mining operations in B.C., Ontario and in Nevada. I am happy to say that the government of Manitoba has removed some of these restrictive taxes on mining operations in northern Manitoba so we shall certainly see an improvement in Manitoba. But Manitoba cannot cure all of Canada's economic ills on its own.
The Senate also heard a tax expert, a gentleman by the name of Mr. R. D. Brown. According to the Senate study-
-Mr. Brown considered the Canadian tax structure as inefficient. After the detailed comparative study of the tax systems in Canada, United States and northern Europe for one industry, he concluded that the Canadian system imposed more burdens on its industry than the tax systems of other countries. As to its effect on competitiveness, Mr. Brown said: "Our tax system does not help and indeed hinders the aggregate level of productivity in Canada and tends to make our products have a more difficult time in world markets".
What are we doing about these things? Absolutely nothing. All we are doing is talking about a bill to enable the government to borrow more money. Isn't that a great solution to all our problems? You borrow more money, print more money, spend more money. I should have brought along some of the speeches made in days gone by by the hon. member for Crowfoot, because they would have made an excellent contribution to this debate. I looked up some of his old speeches on the devalued dollar. Some of his comments are worth repeating.
Yesterday I asked the Minister of Finance a question about the amount of investment money currently leaving the country. The volume of investment money leaving the country has now reached record proportions. I asked what steps would be taken to encourage investors to stay in Canada. In reply we were given the typical, gobbledygook answer that the minister is reducing taxes by $2 billion. He is not even making an effort to meet with these people to Find out why they will not invest in Canada. He is taking a totally negative approach.
We have also heard detailed speeches about the socialist policies we have in this country today. This is a comment made by Mr. Rowland Frazee, President of the Royal Bank of Canada, as reported in the Free Press:
Borrowing Authority Act
Foreign investors are not investing in Canada because they hold a dated perception that Canada is left-leaning and unreliable, says Rowland C. Frazee, President of the Royal Bank of Canada.
Frazee said it would probably take another year for outside investors to realize Canada has now implemented orthodox economic policies in a bid to shore up the dollar and hold down inflation.
Mr. Frazee feels that everything will be straightened out in another year, but we will have to wait to see about that.
With regard to the public debt which the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary secretary made light of, I would like to give a few statistics. The wild spending habits of the government have resulted in steadily mounting deficits. When the government borrows money to pay for the deficits, the public debt increases. Gross public debt has doubled since the Prime Minister took office, rising from $32.9 billion in 1968 to $67.1 billion in 1977.
I understand that the latest figures show that it is heading toward $90 billion or $98 billion. It took the present Prime Minister and this government only ten years to double the public debt. Before the Prime Minister and this government came to office it took 23 years to double the public debt. This government has increased the public debt at a rate faster than any government in Canada's peacetime history. Gross public debt increased by $7.3 billion in 1977. That increase is greater than the total public debt of 1942.
I am sure Canadian taxpayers would be interested to know that interest payments on this debt have skyrocketed. In 1968 the federal government spent $1.3 billion to pay for accumulated debts. In the coming financial year $6.5 billion will be spent, Five times the amount of 1968. Federal debt costs were $62 for every Canadian in 1968. Now they are $278, four and one-half times greater. When does the end come? Every time we have another of these bills before us we hear a series of excuses that everything is in order and going great. The deeper the government gets into debt, the greater it says things are. What a philosophy!
When the federal government issues bonds, bills and securities to pay for its deFicits, they are bought by either private citizens and corporations or by the Bank of Canada. Sales to the private sector place a burden on capital markets by increasing the demand for funds. Federal borrowing requirements of the current size, $8.8 billion, makes it harder for the productive sectors of our economy to borrow funds to finance job-creating investment projects. Sales to the Bank of Canada are paid for by the bank by printing money. In effect, the government owes money to itself, so hon. members can see the ridiculous situation we are in. Too much money in the economic system means inflation. I could go on and on with statistics, but I do not think I have to say any more to get the message across.
There is much comment across Canada today placing the blame on one man. The Prime Minister of Canada must bear a large share of the responsibility because he has handed everyone in his cabinet a blank cheque. Cabinet ministers can do anything they want. They can fly around in JetStars and take all their friends to Grey Cup games. As soon as the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sports) (Mrs. Campagnolo)

October 19, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
became a cabinet minister, she took a JetStar across the Atlantic Ocean and flew around Europe at a cost to taxpayers of about $350,000. She certainly has all the necessary qualifications to be in this Liberal cabinet, and she demonstrated that in short order.
However, we cannot place all the blame on one man. All cabinet ministers are guilty, and even backbenchers who defend this government's record are guilty. They have been leaving one by one. Some have been speaking up while others have just gone off to Bay Street to make a bundle practising law. Mr. Charles Lynch of Southam News summed it up very well as follows:
When we talk about the government being tired and listless, we are talking about the unfaithful departed, like John Turner-
I will get to him in just a minute.
-and Donald Macdonald and Ron Basford, and a host of ministers who have remained on board without pulling their weight-Allan MacEachen, Don Jamieson, Otto Lang, Alastair Gillespie and the faceless ones like Hugh Faulkner, Judd Buchanan, Bud Cullen, John Roberts and Tony Abbott.
That is a great piece of theory about this cabinet, and it is right on.
It is a measure of the government's bankruptcy that Trudeau must now contemplate strengthening his cabinet for the long winter's run to the polls, and he has no place to turn for strength. There is manifestly better cabinet material on the Tory benches than on the Grit side.
It is certain that we have no shortage of talent on this side.
A column by Dennis Braithwaite appeared this week in the Toronto Star in which it is stated:
Since my political predictions are running well ahead of the regular pundits (they are saying today what I said on Aug. 8, that Trudeau's had it), I must press on with further enlightening analyses.
Many Liberals are saying that Mr. Turner must return. Mr. Turner is just as guilty as all of them. I would like to point out that under Mr. John Turner as minister of finance federal government spending increased by 99 per cent in his short term. To put it another way, it took us 105 years to reach a federal spending level of $17.4 billion. John Turner doubled that figure in 44 months, taking the level of government spending in his brief term-

They may have been reading obituaries, but some of them are imaginary. They get up with their books and read many things which all of us have read and discarded. I do not really think they have been reading the second section of the Globe and Mail or any other business journals because they show that in the last year momentum has slowly been building toward an economic upturn.
This upturn has been engineered by the present government. The Progressive Conservatives are fighting hard to get in on the good times round the corner which have been prepared by us Liberals.

I am quite serious when I say that. There is nothing like listening to the people in your own constituency to find out what is going on. I do not listen to members on the opposite side too often because they are ghost writers really. They have somebody telling them what to say, and then they get up and say it. Actually, I have spent the summer going around my constituency of Welland and I have found that there have never been such good times in Canada, despite the doom and gloom in the media and in the accusations coming from the opposition.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) had a few interesting observations to make. I thought he made the most thoughtful speech today.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
But nothing constructive is coming from the other side. I thought that the financial critic on the other side showed everything except a knowledge of finance. All he did was to deliver a diatribe of accusations. He referred to all sorts of things that had no substance to back up his statements.
Let me get back to speaking about my own riding, which I respect and for which I have a great affection. I have done a lot of work there, and I think they appreciate it. I have visited several manufacturing firms in my riding. We have been told that manufacturing is down to 80 per cent of its capacity. That is completely untrue; they are at full capacity, most of them running two, sometimes three shifts.
We have heard talk that the government is not sufficiently subsidizing research and development. My God, what do they want? Do they want us to supply everything? Business in Canada is just waking up to the knowledge that they have to put some effort into it too. We have been pampering them. Research and development in most Canadian firms is increasing, partly because the firms are starting to realize that they must supply 1 per cent to 3 per cent of total sales in order to become competitive. This entails some hard times for two or three years, but they are facing up to the challenge.
I have found also that exports from my riding, although they are sometimes only 10 per cent, in many cases are in the range
October 19, 1978

of 70 per cent of industrial manufacturing. Millions of dollars from these firms are going into expansion. The money is going into building and machinery. They have more faith in Canada than the other side of the House. I cannot understand the prophets over there talking about Canada going to the devil when our Canadian manufacturers are saying that things have been definitely on the upswing for the last six or 12 months and are getting better all the time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
What is more, they have competitive ability. Our firms are selling products in the United States which they could not begin to sell two or three years ago. Why is it? Is it because of this weak, sick, Canadian dollar? Ha, just think of that! What is the matter with you men over there? Do you not realize that this is what is giving us much of our competitive edge and this is what the manufacturers want? Just because people cannot go on trips to Europe or to the United States and buy everything cheaply over there like they can at home- most of it is not important to their standard of living or way of life-do you think that people do not realize that Canadian prosperity hinges on our exports?
Now that the Canadian dollar is down, our companies will continue to be prosperous. What is more, those firms tell me they do not want to see the dollar get any closer than 10 cents or 12 cents to the U.S. dollar. I wish I had not bought American currency a couple of days ago. A lot of ridiculous nonsense has been said about the dollar. It is about time we realized the exchange rate is in our favour and that we are benefiting from it. Let us hope it does not go up closer to the American dollar than 90 cents.
When I think of the different companies in my riding I am reminded of the textile industries which have had so much trouble because of the third world, and we have to expect it. Yet Canada with her negotiations in GATT has done a great deal for these textile industries. Mr. Fyfe through my efforts was able to meet with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) last spring. I think now that they feel they can make things go, it is possible they will get about 50 per cent or 60 per cent of the domestic market in Canada, which is what they must have if they are to survive. Also, there is John Deere in the Welland area. It is a U.S. firm, but it is unique in the fact that it makes millions of dollars worth of sales every year. There is no other company that does exactly that type of manufacturing in the U.S., so they can compete and export to the United States. In fact, they have sent 70 per cent of their manufactured goods to the United States, which will certainly improve our export trade balance. Every year they spend 3 per cent on research and development. They are really a great asset to Canada. In the next year or two that company will spend between $5 million and $15 million on expansion.
Another company is Union Carbide which is going to spend $5 million to $20 million next year on expansion. It exports 5 per cent to 6 per cent of its products, although it covers the Canadian market to a large degree.
Borrowing Authority Act
Then we have Stelco, which was a big company before the pipeline business started. They built a nine-acre plant two years ago in readiness for the pipeline, but they have not got it going yet. However, not to worry; Stelco is doing all right even selling material in the U.S., Mexico and other places. Their competitive ability is excellent. So let hon. members not talk to me about a country which is going down the drain. Stelco is ready to put out a mile of pipe a day when they get the orders.
Then we have Atlas Steel, one of the great steel companies in Welland. They wrote me a letter the other day thanking the government for all it had tried to do in the GATT negotiations and in the anti-dumping tribunals. That company feels it has been fairly treated, even though it did not get all it wanted. At least Atlas indicated that it hoped we would continue to make sure dumping did not occur. I know the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is doing his best to prevent it.
We have received a lot of criticism from the other side concerning the takeover of Canadian companies by American companies. I should like to refer to the Mansfield-Denman Company in Welland which was dying by inches because its parent company in the United States did not have enough capital to enlarge, refurbish its machinery and modernize. That was the case until the Foreign Investment Review Agency took on the problem and recognized that the applicant, General Tire, had the ability and financial capacity to enlarge that plant's output for export in Welland, as well as its tire plant in Barrie, Ontario. The Welland plant exports a great deal. In fact, it manufactures canister components for gas masks for the Canadian, American and German defence forces. That firm is prospering.
The Hayes-Dana Company is situated in an area of Ontario which is shared by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Parent), the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Young), the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Andres) and myself. Until recently that firm employed 800 people; now it has increased its staff by another 800 people. Basically it is situated in the St. Catharines area, and Welland is the bedroom component of that industry. As well it has increased its staff by a few hundred in the new plant in Barrie.
Can one say that I have told a sad story about Canadian industry? There are small firms in Welland, many forge plants which supply the bigger plants. Recently I received a telephone call from the manager of General Forge. His firm has been successful in getting capital in order to enlarge by $2 million to build some additional plant and refurbish the existing plant because it is exporting a great deal now.
It is time for optimism in the House. I spoke tonight because I have heard so much pessimism and ridiculous accusations against the government. One would think the country is going down the drain. Canada has never had it so good. Sometimes I require loans just like everyone else, so I have had occasion to speak with bankers. It provides me with an opportunity to hear their ideas. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who preceded me referred to opposition parties spelling doom and gloom, and to the result of their talking about the devalued dollar and the fall of the government. I should like to refer to a few comments made by a former minister of finance, the Hon. Mitchell Sharp, back in May of 1962. He said that the Canadian dollar, once the strongest currency in the world, was in danger of becoming known as the Diefendollar in which, like the Diefenbaker government, there was less and less public confidence. He said that when the government lost control of the exchange, was forced to abandon its policies and devalue the currency, the country would be in serious peril. The dollar was at 92.5 cents at that time. What would it be like now that the dollar is worth 82.5 cents? Also he indicated that it was one thing to reduce the value of the Canadian dollar deliberately in order to assist our trading position, but it was quite another thing when the Canadian dollar is forced down because the world has lost confidence in our economy and financial policies.
Bill C-7 was given first reading in the House approximately two days ago. It seeks a $7 billion supplementary borrowing authority for the rest of the current fiscal year, and a further $10 billion borrowing authority for the fiscal year 1980. 1 could not even consider giving my consent to the borrowing of some $17 billion until I know just how the money is to be spent.
For quite some time now I have wanted to express some of my concerns and feelings about why this government is in the position that it now has to borrow more money and become involved in a hodgepodge of cutbacks. The major economic statement we heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on August 1 really boils down to what I can only call a hodgepodge of cutbacks involving some $2 billion in spending and the elimination of 5,000 jobs in the public sector. It also involves the freezing of new public service hirings.
This government's attempt at restraint is certainly welcome. However, this announcement, impromptu as it was, resulted in ministers of the Crown scurrying back to Ottawa to determine just where the cuts should be made. This is no surprise to me in view of the mismanagement we have seen in respect of government spending over the past ten years. I am not surprised that there have to be cutbacks because this government's spending has been out of control, particularly for the last five years.
Let me devote my remarks to one area of the Churchill constituency which I am proud to represent. If the Liberals are really serious about restraint, why does the government not sell the empty government houses in Churchill, Manitoba, or at least make every effort to prevent a further white elephant such as the Otineka Mall and Churchill complex? I will deal specifically with this as I get further into my remarks.
October 19, 1978

What happened in the town of Churchill on the Hudson Bay coast in Manitoba is a prime example of what this government has been doing. For over three centuries Churchill has been a base for explorers, scientists and travellers. It is also one of the main grain handling ports in Canada. In the last century this community has become the subject of government whim.
Let me go back to 1969 when an agreement was reached between the NDP government of Manitoba and the federal Liberal government of Canada to embark on a 13-point plan for the redevelopment of the townsite of Churchill. At that time there were some 4,000 people living in the community of Churchill. I have never been able to pin down who the architect of this redevelopment plan was. I have tried unsuccessfully by inquiring of the Department of Public Works and of various other offices.
At the time government officials felt that a viable tax base existed in Churchill to support an estimated $32 million redevelopment plan. From 1969 to 1976 the redevelopment plan was carried out. Just two years ago a multimillion dollar recreational complex was opened in Churchill. The complex cost $13 million, $8 million of which was put up by the federal government and $5 million by the NDP government of Manitoba. It was based on a population of 4,000 at that time. Someone in government did not realize that the population of Churchill in 1976 had decreased to some 1,700 or 1,800.
Under the roof of this huge, monstrous complex there exists a paramedical and dental care facility, an arena, a gymnasium, a four-sheet curling rink with artificial ice, bowling alleys, a swimming pool, theatres, a skating rink with artificial ice, and, lo and behold, in the rotunda of this complex in the frozen tundra of Churchill we have $100,000 worth of tropical plants, along with benches and all the facilities of a park. You can walk around inside this area. As I say, at the time of completion we had exactly 1,700 people living in the community.
In addition to these facilities this huge complex housed a high school designed to facilitate the education of 300 students. In 1977 there were 100 students attending that high school, at a cost of $180,000 per year. That is what it cost to educate those 100 students. Today there are 55 high school students attending school in that complex, and it still costs something in the neighbourhood of $150,000 or $160,000 to educate those students. This complex is like an albatross or a yoke around the necks of the people who live in the Churchill community.
The population in Churchill today is 1,400. That is an example of how this federal government has done its planning, how it squanders the taxpayers' money. The government pays no attention whatever to what is going on in northern Manitoba. This is only one example of how this government squanders the taxpayers' money, in this case to the extent of $8 million in federal funds. The people of Churchill would have been happy with a $1 million building designed in such a way that it could be utilized by the local population. Today you could fire a cannon in that place and never hit anyone. This complex is so huge it costs $1,200,000 a year just to maintain it and there are only 1,400 in the community.

When the complex was started, or shortly thereafter, this government began to reduce the armed services in Churchill. Churchill was a winter training area. Then the government pulled the National Research Council out of Churchill and moved it to Gimli, Manitoba. I asked why and was told that it was too costly to continue operations in Churchill. This was after they commenced building this $13 million recreation complex. The government has now said to the people that this complex is its gift to the people of Churchill: 'There it is, now you look after it".
In addition to pulling out the armed services and the National Research Council, the government pulled the CBC employees out of the community. This amounted to a loss of 16 jobs in that community. I could never figure out why the CBC needed 16 people to run a radio station in Churchill where there was a population of 1,400 people, but I suppose that is a pretty good ratio in order to give good radio programming. This has left the community with a recreation complex it cannot afford. The new Conservative government of Manitoba has given a grant to continue maintaining the complex for at least this year. I do not know what will happen after this year. I have in front of me a newspaper clipping with a heading "A Dream Dies at Churchill, Can't Explain Where People Went, say Planners of Facelift". The article reads in part:
"You can go up to the centre and fire a cannon and you wouldn't hit anybody," laments Jack O'Connor, vice president of the local chamber of commerce.
The desolate Hudson Bay outpost is stirring with a California-style tax revolt. In order to maintain the centre, local taxes have gone up 24 per cent in the last year.
Later, the article goes on:
Troubleshooters in the federal-provincial relations section of the Privy Council office in Ottawa have been asked to find a solution-and the solution could mean an infusion of more tax money.
The government came up with a proposal to put money in there but they have not bothered with it since. The cost of this redevelopment of Churchill has skyrocketed. It was estimated at $32 million but cost closer to $50 million.
There was also redevelopment of housing in Churchill. The federal government owns 80 per cent of these homes and it rebuilt them. I do not know where the government finds the architects for this work when it is required in remote areas of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. They must be good Liberal supporters. The buildings are so overdesigned that it takes three or four times longer than usual to construct them.
I have the example of someone, a painter, who went to Churchill to do some contract work in one of the 20-unit apartment buildings. His experience shows that money is of no concern to the government. Indeed, if the government had any commonsense at all the $2 billion restraint program might not have been necessary. Government waste alone could probably account for $2 billion without the other cutbacks and lay-offs of public servants. This painter who went to Churchill on a contract says that a simple two-day job lasted six days because the paint was either the wrong kind, the wrong colour or was

October 19, 1978

not even available. Much of it had to be mixed in order to match the architect's specifications. Colours selected were difficult to apply-yellow numbers on dark orange doors required four coats to cover instead of two if dark numbers on a light background had been chosen. Twelve stripes on one wall required twelve different colours and consequently 12 quarts of paint, yet only half a quart was used in total.
There were architects' specification sheets, a fully detailed print, in scale, for every two apartment doors, indicating the actual number and its location on the door with angles and measurements in fractions of an inch-a total of 12 sheets. These are architects' blueprints of V/i feet by 3'A feet. This is what I call government waste.
This particular apartment has 20 suites and has taken almost three years to build. Initially the cost was estimated at $250,000 and ended at perhaps $750,000. This was a government cost-sharing project with the government of Manitoba and there was no concern about controlling the expenditures. Contractors and architects were allowed to spend money like water because it was taxpayers' money.
Although almost ready for occupancy, the doors were binding because the building had already moved; the roof was leaking; exterior paint was peeling because primer had not been used properly; walls were painted after carpet was installed leaving marks on the carpet and some walls were painted seven times because painting quality was rejected.
Other apartments and houses had similar problems. Cedar siding was imported thousands of miles and the protective coating that was applied was simply eaten away by the salt water air. Why not use local rocks or stones instead that would stand up against salt water air instead of shipping in cedar siding?
The government's move to restraint will mean nothing until their actual plans are monitored. If they are unable to do so themselves then it is time they considered the value of local input. While the government mouths restraint, as many as 40 government housing units stand empty in Churchill. There is a waiting list for rental accommodation there from residents who do not have proper accommodation.
I want to explain about this government housing, Mr. Speaker. I have in front of me a file entitled "Pool Housing". I know the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) has encountered exactly the same situation in his area. A 1956 Treasury Board Order No. 1301 specifies that "local hires"-meaning someone hired from the community-are not entitled to government housing. A resident of Churchill could not live in a government house if he was hired locally. If the Department of Public Works, the National Research Council or the Department of Tranport went to any other community in the country, they could hire someone there, take them to Churchill and supply them with government housing if it was available.
This redevelopment program which cost $50 million must have supplied 80 to 90 units in Churchill. When I asked what those units were for, the answer I got from Treasury Board

was that the Department of Transport pays for a certain number of units on an annual basis, so does the CBC, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the National Research Council and three or four other departments. Ironically, even though the accommodation was being paid for, no one was living in it.
When I started inquiring into this in 1976, I got nowhere. I was told that all units were full. I contacted the CBC, DOT and NRC, and they claimed to be using these facilities. People in Churchill have told me, however, that 40 or 50 of these units are empty all the time. Taxpayers pay to heat these units and to maintain them-all for nothing. They are empty. There is not a soul living in them, yet there are people living in Churchill without a roof over their head.
Now, lo and behold, after many letters to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), we were successful in having local hires in Churchill get government housing. That means if someone can qualify for a job in Churchill they can now qualify for government housing. This is ironic, Mr. Speaker, because since 1956 a local hire could not get a government house. This success was accomplished only by a lot of hard work, because the first letter I received from the Treasury Board said: "Here are the regulations, we must abide by them. We cannot make any changes because this is all set out by the President of the Treasury Board." My last letter was written in August. The letter I received in reply from the President of the Treasury Board says that: "The timing of your letter is most opportune. As an officer of the Treasury Board Secretariat I am presently reviewing the continuous issue of local hires. I have requested that your further concerns that federally-owned apartments are standing vacant in Churchill while public servants in the community face a general accommodation shortage be incorporated in that study."
He goes on to say that there is a study under way and local hires will have accommodation, and they are going to sell the houses they do not need now. These houses have been surplus for the last five years. No one has lived in them. But now, all of a sudden they will be sold. I tell hon. members it is evident there is an election just around the corner because some of the letters that members write to the President of the Treasury Board are now being answered. I thought I should touch briefly on the housing situation in Churchill.
As I have said before, here is a community with the best grain handling facilities in Canada which are being underutilized because this government, with their cat and mouse games, will not increase shipping through Churchill. The Hall commission report says the port of Churchill can handle 55 million bushels of grain with little or no extra expense. This government is still pussyfooting around. It is not even bothering to put that amount of grain through Churchill.
The cat and mouse game that they have been playing with Churchill leads me into my next remarks. After the Hall commission report was released, our flying minister-"Twin-Otto Lang" I call him-has to commission a report from
October 19, 1978

Bryden Development Consultants Western Limited of Winnipeg. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, who Bryden is? He used to work for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). 1 believe he was a secretary or something for the minister.

speechtext: A bag man.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Yes, a bag man. So another report is commissioned for Churchill because the minister did not believe the Hall report, or did not want to believe it. The Saskatoon Star Phoenix reported on March 11, 1978, that the federal grains group was aware of the firm's view that the development of the Hudson Bay port was uneconomical when it commissioned the study. The study referred to is the Bryden report. They just spelled gloom and doom for Churchill. Talk about the Conservatives spelling gloom and doom! Mr. Speaker, I think I am a very positive person, but it is impossible trying to be positive with a government that is so inept. I have to be a little bit negative. They will not be around here in another seven months or so, but we do not need to dwell on that.
The Hall commission report dealt with the shipment of some 55 million bushels of grain through the port, as I mentioned before. The port of Churchill this year was strikebound for 13 days. This meant that ships that were originally destined for Churchill were diverted to Montreal, to Halifax, and some to Thunder Bay. It meant that some 7 million to 9 million bushels of grain which was supposed to be shipped out of Churchill took the route through Thunder Bay. What has this done to the port of Churchill? It has placed the port of Churchill in a cash loss position. That port must have shipment of at least 25 million bushels of grain per annum in order to break even. This year only 23 million bushels have gone through that port.
We understand the government is in a bind and because of that they do not have the grain moving in Canada. I do not know if they will ever get it moving, but they have scheduled the m.v. Arctic, which is a Canadian class II ice-breaker, to go to Churchill on November 15 to pick up a cargo of grain, and for that I compliment the government. This is the latest date that any ship has gone into Churchill because the season there closes on October 23. Incidentally the river at Churchill is now frozen and full of slob ice at this particular time.
However, in view of the fact that the lakehead is now affected by a strike, resulting in no grain movement through there, I asked the government if it would consider directing the Wheat Board, if it wants to have grain moving, to have at least four or five other ships go in with the m.v. Arctic to Churchill and move out another 4 million or 5 million bushels of grain. As well I requested that at least 4 million bushels of grain which has already been sold for next year's shipments be stored. It could be stored at Churchill. The port of Churchill has the most ideal storage conditions anywhere in Canada. It is like a permanent deep freeze in the wintertime. Humidity is not a problem.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43 and also during question period a few days ago I raised the problem of the chaotic state of Canada's grain transport system, which has caused a backlog of 4 million metric tons of grain worth $450 million still to be shipped if Canada is to meet its 1978 commitments.
Prairie grain elevators are close to overflowing. Their grain stocks are up 35 per cent from a year ago. At the same time, grain stocks at the major export terminals are down 33 per cent from last year. The problem is not that farmers have suddenly dumped their grain at the country elevator in the last few weeks as deliveries to primary elevators are also lagging behind 1977 figures. The tie-up is in rail movement of grain to export positions.
The government spent $800,000 in upgrading the port of Churchill this past summer. Rail trackage has increased and the Herchmer subdivision siding is now in service providing a passing track and lessening turnaround time for the grain cars. Moreover, Churchill has storage capacity for 4 million bushels of grain and the natural advantages of constant freezing temperatures and low humidity. Regardless of these advantages and improvements, the federal government refuses to increase grain shipments through Churchill and fully utilize the Manitoba port.
A wildcat strike by CNR yardmen and brakemen at Thunder Bay blocked grain traffic to the terminals in late September. Now, a strike by licensed seamen on the Great Lakes has left ships harboured and loaded grain cars idle. Shipowners are saying it will be too costly to reactivate ships with less than eight weeks left in the shipping season.
The government has a commitment to their overseas markets that it is failing to meet. In view of the natural advantages of the port of Churchill and the present situation in Thunder Bay, will the government redirect grain cars now standing idle at Thunder Bay to Churchill? Ships could be diverted from the St. Lawrence Seaway to follow the new Canadian icebreaker m.v. Arctic. During the 13-day strike by grainhandlers at the port of Churchill this past summer, ships were diverted to the eastern seaports. Why will the government not follow the same policy now in order to put that port on a cash saving basis?
The Hudson Bay port is down 7 million to 9 million bushels in grain shipments this year over last year and is in a cash-loss position. Does the minister responsible for the Wheat Board not have the foresight and initiative to move the loaded grain

October 19, 1978
Adjournment Debate
cars now filling the rail yard at Thunder Bay? Why not utilize the 4 million bushel storage facilities at Churchill? The Wheat Board has confirmed grain shipments through the port for next year and could store grain here ready for shipment in the spring. This would remove the port from a cash-loss position and ensure its continued operation. This is very important because, if it is in a cash-loss position, the loss must be borne by the federal government. Therefore, why not ship more grain through this port and put it in a cash saving position?
The government gives with one hand and takes with the other. After upgrading facilities, and now, assigning the m.v. Arctic to chart Hudson Bay waters as late as November 15, which will be an historic voyage, in an effort to extend the season, the government refuses to increase our throughput or use existing storage facilities.
The Hall Commission on grain handling and transportation recommended development of the port of Churchill and an increase in grain shipments to 55 million bushels. Not satisfied with the report's conclusions, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) commissioned a second study, the Bryden report, which views further development as uneconomical.
This government jumps from one side of the fence to the other, never landing long enough on one side to leave even the faintest of footprints. When will the present Liberal government take a stand and commit itself to the development of this western port? There are only a few months left.

Mr. Speaker, we are happy to see that the hon. member realizes the efforts the government has made to allow the port of Churchill to reach full development. I would like to point out that for 1978 alone we spent more than $5,575,000 on equipment for that port.
The Canadian Wheat Board also showed its willingness to use the port of Churchill as much as possible. Record volumes of grain were moved through that part in recent years and it is conceivable that a new record would have been set this year had it not been for last summer's unfortunate strike.
The government is pleased with the efforts that have been made to make better use of that port but we would not want, and we would think it would be inappropriate, to interfere in the operation of the Canadian Wheat Board by giving it, for example, instruction on its storage policy. Its job is to analyze the market and direct grains so as to maximize producers' profits. It does so by considering all relevant factors, including the availability of land and water means of transport at any given time. It is empowered to do so, and we do not think we should be taking its place in this area. The board is quite aware of the advantages of using the port of Churchill. We have full confidence in its judgment as far as making maximum use of that port. The fact is that the board stored 3.8 million bushels of grain in that port last winter.

If that is to its advantage the board may decide again to store grain there next winter. On the other hand, it may decide on a better use to be made of the railway rolling stock and direct the grain toward other ports where ships are also available. It is up to it to decide, and I repeat that it would be inappropriate to interfere in its affairs. Indeed, the hon. member would be the first one to complain if the minister were to give instructions to the board on a daily basis. I believe for that matter that western producers have faith in the board's judgment and they would prefer not to have us interfere in its every day business.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-HIRING OF CONSULTANTS OUTSIDE CANADA-POSSIBILITY OF CHARGES BEING LAID
AIR TRANSPORT-HIRING OF CONSULTANTS OUTSIDE CANADA-POSSIBILITY OF CHARGES BEING LAID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to follow up a question I asked in the House on October 16. I put my first question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) and then addressed the supplementary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson). The subject was moneys which has been paid by Boeing to consultants in Canada as part of a practice commonly known as fraud or graft.
I considered the answers given to me to be unsatisfactory. The Minister of National Defence said a year and a half ago that if there was any evidence of impropriety he would cause an investigation to be launched. My supplementary question was as follows:
Certainly there is evidence of impropriety at the present time, which impropriety has been known for over two months since the Boeing revelations. What have the results of the investigation been? Who is in charge of it?
The minister replied:
At the time the issue was looked into and we could not find any evidence, record or indication of any impropriety involving Canadians or from Boeing itself.
I do not know where the minister has been spending his time if he sees no evidence of impropriety. The Citizen in August carried this headline: "Boeing pay-off scheme cites Canadian sales". Southam News Services said: "Canadian jet sales part of dual contract pay-offs". Further headlines said: "Boeing files on consultants"; "Selling aircraft under the table". The Vancouver Sun has the same story. There is the comment in the Victoria Daily Colonist, "Who got what from Boeing?"
Then the other day, following my question in the House the Canadian Press reported:
Defence Minister Danson says the government has uncovered no evidence of wrongdoing by Canadians in Boeing aircraft sales.
The reference was not just to the department. It was to the Canadian government generally.
I should like to quote from the original source of these revelations, form 8K which was filed in response to the civil injunction against Boeing by the securities and exchange commission in the United States. When this injunction came before the court, Boeing and the securities and exchange commission made a deal that Boeing would report on the
October 19, 1978

As you probably know, Mr. Speaker, it is not unusual for companies to use agents to promote their interests. This is a common business practice and there is nothing basically wrong about it. On the other hand, it is not basically illegal for such an agent, even if he is a Canadian as in the present case, to receive his commission or his fees outside Canada, for instance in a foreign bank account, to the extent that this agent does not do so in an attempt to evade taxes, and of course, in this case, it is the Department of Revenue which would be responsible for protecting the interests of Canada or for ensuring that the fees received by this agent are not used illegally, especially by diverting the money received from the seller to an agent of the purchaser.
Following the allegations reported in March 1977 by several Canadian media, the Canadian government examined this whole matter very thoroughly. On March 15, 1977, as the hon. member said earlier, the attorneys general of Canada and the United Stated reached an agreement to allow Canadian and American police forces to co-operate closely in an examination of this matter and in making a detailed investigation to check whether there had been illegal use of the sums in question and whether there had really been illegal payments. Following this agreement, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police carried out a thorough investigation to determine whether one or more Boeing agents had used the sums received by this company for prohibited purposes. I may say to hon. members that the

October 19, 1978
Adjournment Debate
RCMP carried out this investigation most conscientiously and that it seems to be just about ready to report its conclusions.
I must point out to the hon. member that it would be preferable to wait for the investigation to be completed and for the results to be referred to the Attorney General of Canada so that he can determine whether or not these funds have been used illegally and exonerate the people involved if there is no appearance of illegality, or, of course, if there are indications of illegal use, lay charges against those who have committee irregular actions. I therefore suggest to the hon. member that if he can be patient, he will soon be satisfied one way or another.

subtopic: FISHERIES-PROPOSED TRANSFER OF WEATHER FORECASTING SERVICES
FISHERIES-PROPOSED TRANSFER OF WEATHER FORECASTING SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday I put the following question to the environment minister.
In light of the recent announcement by the Department of the Environment that there will be a cut in weather forecasting services in Newfoundland and Labrador, a decision which will seriously endanger the lives and safety of thousands of fishermen who operate off the Newfoundland coast, and in view of the minister's announcement that weather forecasting services in Newfoundland and Labrador will be transferred to Halifax, can the minister assure this House unequivocally that the weather forecasting services will not be transferred to Halifax, and can he further assure the House that there will be no cut in weather forecasting services off the Newfoundland coast?
Since the minister was not in the House, I did not receive an answer. I think that certain actions by the Department of the Environment need to be explained to the people of Newfoundland, and indeed to all the people living in Atlantic Canada. These actions include the reduction of weather forecasting from four times a day to twice a day.
The minister may not realize it, but there are 20,000 licensed fishermen in Newfoundland whose safety and livelihood depend on the accuracy and frequency of marine weather forecasts. Furthermore, search and rescue services for Newfoundland and Labrador based at Gander have publicly admitted their service would be hampered by the change. This, of course, also jeopardizes the safety of fishermen and others who ply those seas. The minister should rescind these cutbacks immediately.
Second, the Department of the Environment has announced a cutback in the ice reconnaissance program to the tune of $1.8 million. Again, surely you must recognize the importance and necessity of ice movement information for fishing and shipping in the early spring. This downgrading of the service can only be detrimental to the safety of all those who sail the seas off the Newfoundland coast. There is no alternative for the ministry but to withdraw these cutback announcements.
Also, the officials of the department announced the shifting of weather forecasting services from Gander to Halifax. It is a callous and ill-advised decision as it will disrupt lives and impair the safety of those who depend on frequent and accurate weather forecasts. Moreover, there is ample evidence that

these moves will not result in the kinds of savings which our bureaucrats envisage. I call on the minister now to withdraw that decision.
Another cutback which although not directly connected to the Department of the Environment has serious implications for Environment Canada is the laying off of dll employees at the Bonavista Ministry of Transport communications office. Approximately six Department of Transport employees with 25 'h. years of service received their lay-off notices last week, which notices are to be effective on February 24, 1979. These men supplied hourly weather reporting services on a 24-hour basis, seven days a week. The information was supplied to the Gander weather office for the compiling of marine weather forecasts.
It is true that they are declared redundant because computers can do their jobs as defined by the Department of Transport. But one must remember they provide direct contact with weather forecasters on an hourly basis. Also one must remember that the unemployment rate in that province is the highest of any part of the country. The Department of Transport indicated that it was a problem for the Department of Fisheries and the Environment, and that their jobs with the Department of Transport are finished. It is the minister's responsibility to ensure that this very valuable weather information is not lost to those who depend on knowing these conditions for their safety and livelihood.
Also I should like to refer to the fact that a weather office in Corner Brook was promised approximately one and a half years ago. Can the minister inform the House as to the status of that project? Also the environment centre which is presently under construction in St. John's was cut by $2.2 million. I hope the minister can tell us whether the project is still on schedule, and if it is, when it is to be completed.
I understand from the rumour mill and hearsay that on the evening of October 11, which was the eve of the by-election in Newfoundland, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) made an announcement in that province indicating that all of these decisions had been rescinded. He indicated that the weather reporting would continue and that the office would not be moved from Gander to Halifax. Perhaps that decision may have been tinged by the fact that the by-election in that province was approximately five days away. At the present time the people most concerned with these problems have not received any official word from the Department of Fisheries and the Environment. The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) should rise and tell us of the decision. He does not seem to know what is going on in his department.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs was making his announcement in Newfoundland, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment was travelling around western Canada in an attempt to keep Liberal Saskatchewan on the map. It is his responsibility to let us know what is the disposition of these particular matters.
October 19, 1978

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Pearsall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-PROPOSED TRANSFER OF WEATHER FORECASTING SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) here this evening. I waited last Thursday night until 10.30 p.m., but he failed to show. I did not know whether he intended to raise his question tonight. However, he made a number of statements, and I should like to point out that his conclusions concerning statements made by people other than the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) do not pertain to this issue.
Although the Department of Fisheries and the Environment is faced with major and serious budget reductions, the minister would like to assure the House, in order to maintain the highest possible level of weather services for Newfoundland and Labrador, that he has decided weather forecasting services will not be transferred to Halifax but will continue to be

provided, as in the past, from the Gander weather office. Despite what the hon. member said, the minister has instructed the atmospheric environment service to ensure that the
quality of weather services in Newfoundland and Labrador is maintained at current levels. Specifically he directed that there be no cutback in the number of daily weather forecasts for the province and adjacent waters.
The hon. member should give proper notice to the minister on the other matters which he raised. I am sure the minister would be prepared to answer them.
